subtopic: MR. HOWARD  RESPONSIBILITY OF JUSTICE MINISTER UNDER BILL OF RIGHTS
MR. HOWARD  RESPONSIBILITY OF JUSTICE MINISTER UNDER BILL OF RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question of privilege involving the duties and responsibilities of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chevrier) and what I think is a violation of the responsibilities which he has. Section 3 of the Canadian Bill of Rights reads as follows:
The Minister of Justice shall-[DOT]
So it is not discretionary; he must do this.
-in accordance with such regulations as may be prescribed by the governor in council, examine every proposed regulation submitted in draft form to the Clerk of the Privy Council pursuant to the Regulations Act and every bill introduced in or presented to the House of Commons, in order to ascertain whether any of the provisions thereof are inconsistent with the purposes and provisions of this part and he shall report any such inconsistency to the House of Commons at the first convenient opportunity.
Then there are regulations pursuant to that section which merely set out more intricate machinery as to how this should be done; it involves a certificate to be signed by the deputy minister, and so on, but I do not think that is germane to this point at the moment.
On June 7 of this year, more than six months ago, I introduced in this house Bill No. C-71. The bill was introduced and given first reading, and so far-and I checked this with the office of the Clerk of the House of Commons this morning at about twenty or twenty five minutes after nine o'clock-that bill has not been returned from the Department of Justice with any indication on it that it has been examined.
During the last session, in fact on February 1, I raised a similar question of privilege and founded upon it a motion, which is to be found at page 3329 of Hansard for February 1 last, that the standing committee on privileges and elections be authorized and instructed to inquire into and study the responsibilities attendant upon the Minister of Justice by virtue of section 3 of the Canadian Bill of Rights and whether those responsibilities were properly carried out with respect to Bill C-14, an act respecting Indians. No decision
was taken on that motion. The matter was taken under advisement and the house prorogued, or parliament was dissolved, before an opportunity was accorded the Speaker to rule on it.
There are some interesting comments with respect to that question of privilege reported at page 3330 of Hansard. For example, the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) said:
Mr. Speaker, this appears to us to be a matter of pretty serious import-
Then there is an interjection by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), who said:
A breach of the law; that is all.
Then the hon. member for Laurier continued:
-more particularly because of the fact that the bill has been held up from October 1 until now, and my suggestion to you, sir, is that this matter be taken under advisement.
Then there is the following comment by the then hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin):
Particularly because of the violation of the act by the Minister of Justice.
Precisely the same situation as this arose with respect to Bill No. C-71, and this is even worse because it is a longer period of time, more than six and a half months.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: MR. HOWARD  RESPONSIBILITY OF JUSTICE MINISTER UNDER BILL OF RIGHTS
speechtext: What did the Secretary of State have to say?

subtopic: MR. HOWARD  RESPONSIBILITY OF JUSTICE MINISTER UNDER BILL OF RIGHTS
speechtext:
Unfortunately the Secretary of State was particularly silent when this matter was raised on February 1. I contend that the Minister of Justice has not fulfilled his obligation under the bill of rights with respect to Bill No. C-71. It is immaterial at this stage whether or not, as was done on June 7, the Speaker expresses any thought about the bill, because the measure has been introduced into the House of Commons and given first reading. I remind hon. members of the provisions of section 3 of the bill of rights where the expression is used: "and every bill introduced in, or presented to, the House of Commons", which makes it even broader.
I should like to move a motion founded on this question of privilege, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), namely:
That this house expresses its regret that the Minister of Justice has not fulfilled his obligation pursuant to the Canadian Bill of Rights.

Inquiries of the Ministry

subtopic: MR. HOWARD  RESPONSIBILITY OF JUSTICE MINISTER UNDER BILL OF RIGHTS
speechtext:
I have to decide whether or not there is a question of privilege. I should like to say in this connection first of all that it appears to me that this is rather in the nature of a grievance against the conduct of a minister with regard to action which has or has not been taken. If it is desired to condemn the action of the Minister of Justice it should be done in the form of a substantive motion requiring notice. In this connection I would refer the hon. member to Beauchesne, fourth edition, citation 127, paragraph 2, and to Bourinot at page 301.
In the circumstances it seems to me that the motion is in the nature of a grievance and not a prima facie case of privilege. Therefore I regret I cannot accept the motion.

Mr. Chairman, there is a brief comment I would like to make on item 155, which has to do with the construction or acquisition of buildings for airports under the Department of Transport. My brief reference is to the new airport at Winnipeg, which is indeed a tremendous improvement over the facilities we had there in former years. I regret to say, however, that there is one feature about this airport-as a result, I am told, of the practice of economy-which is unfortunate. I understand that the original plans called for tubes to be provided so that passengers would go from the second level directly out on to the aircraft, but somewhere along the line it was decided that these could not be afforded and they were not installed.
The lay-out of the airport is such that when passengers are going from the airport to the aircraft, or from the aircraft into the airport, both ways they have to go from ground level up, and then down. This is all right for some of us, but for older people, for women with children, for passengers carrying baggage, and so on, it seems rather unfortunate. I know that the first time I went home after the new airport was opened, I went along with the rest and found myself going up to the second level, and when I wanted to get my baggage I had to go down again. I thought I had missed a directional sign or something, but my inquiries revealed that this situation results from a decision taken, on the basis of

economy, not to have these special tubes to permit loading and unloading from the second level.
I can understand this bit of economy, and perhaps we should not get these tubes at Winnipeg for a while yet. But that is not the end of the story. In addition to that, escalators which were planned to operate both ways were altered so that they would go only one way. This means that passengers alighting from aircraft, although they start from ground level, have to walk up to the second floor and then go down to the ground level to get their baggage.
When departing, passengers have to do the same. I hope the department will take another look at this and realize that it is an unfortunate situation, and that if it is not possible to revert to the original plan to have loading from the second level, at least escalators should be installed so that people would not have to walk up a flight of stairs and then down again. I should like to hear from the minister whether consideration is being given to correcting this situation.

Mr. Chairman, while on the subject of international airports I should like to point out to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that the Edmonton building does not suffer from that problem because it is better designed. But one point I would make to the minister which affects all international terminals is that we have a singularly cold reception for people coming into the building off international flights. At European international airports there is a sign which says "Welcome" or "Bienvenue" to the particular country. Why can we not do that here in Canada? I have taken this matter up with the minister's departmental officials on previous occasions and I was told that this should be a local responsibility, that I was to see my local chamber of commerce. These buildings belong to the Department of Transport. Surely in these huge terminals in Edmonton, Winnipeg, Toronto and Montreal we should say "Welcome", even just to welcome Canadians back to their country.
In both languages.

Yes, obviously. At some
terminals we might even go further. After all, here in Ottawa for a certain convenience we use a third language, Spanish.

Mr. Chairman, in answer to the last question I might say that this problem is usually looked after by the local boards of trade. I might inform my hon. friend from Edmonton West that in one area I could mention the local board of trade goes further and meets passengers with a serving of rum.
Supply-Transport
Is the minister suggesting rye and ginger ale here?

However, I will take this point under consideration. With regard to the matter raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, by reason of the earlier cut-back in expenditure in 1962 the installation of the escalators to which the hon. member referred was not proceeded with, but the building is so constructed that escalators can be put in, without requiring many structural changes. I hope that in due course as the situation improves the matter can be taken care of.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: May I ask whether "in due course" will be some time soon? In other words, are plans being made now to reconsider the installation of these escalators?

It depends on the house's treatment of the budget and the estimates, I suppose, but in any event the problem is one to which the department is very much alive. I have also given the matter some consideration myself and am looking forward to visiting the airport in a few days.
With regard to this criticism which has been made of the airport, it is a curious thing but after this rather costly, and I agree rather good, airport was opened it seemed that the criticism made of this matter was rather disproportionate. But in any event the matter is one of some concern, although I cannot give a commitment now as to what the estimates will be next year in this respect.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: I am glad to hear the minister will be coming to Winnipeg. If he will let us know when he is coming we will welcome him with a cup of tea.

Mr. Chairman, I saw in the press not so long ago that the department intends to go ahead with rolling sidewalks at Montreal airport. I know that these rolling sidewalks were included in the original plans for the airport, but there again I am afraid they were the first victims of treasury board in the same way as were the escalators at Winnipeg.
I hope treasury board will revise this policy, because I do not think this sort of thing should be the first to be cut back in any plan for a new public building designed to handle a tremendous number of people boarding or being discharged from an aircraft and who may have parcels in their hands, children with them, and all that. I hope that in any new public building this policy of cutting back on elevators, escalators or rolling sidewalks will be revised. Montreal airport is probably the most beautiful air terminal in the world, yet people are still complaining

Supply-Transport
about the fact that distances between the planes and the public facilities are much too great.
May I ask the minister whether he will give a reply to the question I asked him last night regarding Transair.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We passed that item.

But the minister has not yet
replied. I was hoping that the minister would give a reply to this question.

Mr. Speaker, I should have replied but unfortunately the answer did not come in until after the house met this morning. The situation with Transair is that on part of the route the service in question has been suspended as of January 11. A hearing will take place before the air transport board to consider whether they should permit the air line to abandon this route, at which hearing there will be an opportunity for all interested parties to make representations. Notices of this hearing have been sent out in the usual way.
There is a real problem here, because the traffic load over one part of the route averages out at barely one passenger per trip. Obviously it is not possible to run an air line on that basis on that kind of route without some examination of the problem of how to meet the requirements of the communities involved, and meeting them adequately.
As the matter has not yet been dealt with by the air transport board it would be useless for me to speculate, and quite improper for me to do so, as to what their decision will be until persons making representations have had a full opportunity to do so at the hearing.
There was another part to the hon. member's question, if I remember correctly, concerning Trans-Canada Air Lines transfer of assets or equipment when they abandoned this route. I think I answered this question on July 15 last; there was also an order for return made as well.
But there were no details given.

In any event, the essential point as I have indicated is that Trans-Canada Air Lines equipment is bought and sold in accordance with normal commercial practice. This matter was also before the committee, and I think the report will be found on page 56 and following. Information was sought at that time. I have not had an opportunity to look up the record and see precisely what information was given, but there was an opportunity to ask about it, and there is no information I can give beyond what was given at that point.
[Mr. BalcerJ

I asked if the figures I gave last night were correct, namely that T.C.A. gave to Transair one Viscount, two DC-3's and half a million dollars worth of DC-3 parts for $1. The second question was, will T.C.A. recover any part of this if Transair, who have operated the route for less than a year, gives up the uneconomic part of the line?
The hon. member is really asking me to answer indirectly what I explained to him could not be answered directly.

The minister has in effect told us we shall have to wait until the air transport board holds its hearings, and he says that is the fair thing to do. I suggest it is not the fair thing to leave this matter for the air transport board, because the board itself has already been involved in this whole matter and so has the minister. I am not saying it is the present minister, but some minister has been involved.
It is obvious to all of us who have followed the situation which led to Transair getting this route that at some stage there was a recommendation or intervention at the ministerial level. It was not a case of the air transport board making up its mind as between a couple of carriers. Somewhere there was ministerial intervention, and it was obvious why there had to be. A crown corporation, T.C.A., was involved, and there was an arrangement of some kind-I was about to say a deal, but that might have been invidious. This question of where Transair stands in relation to these routes and to T.C.A. is more than just a matter for the air transport board. There are others involved besides the public and the cities of western Canada. They are the competitors.
What did Mr. McGregor tell us at the committee hearings? He said T.C.A. tried to demonstrate as far as it could that it was impossible to make money on this southern line. Despite all the arguments which T.C.A. gave, Transair insisted that money could be made, and they went ahead. They got in in April, and now they are out. Given a situation of this kind, it is not good enough to say that a solution will come as a result of hearings to be held by the board. There is surely a need for ministerial action and explanation with regard to this matter. If this is not forthcoming, I have to feel that the minister is letting the air transport board carry responsibility for something with regard to which he himself should be reaching a decision.

I should like to say a word or two on the decor of public airport buildings. I know that in the past such questions as these have usually been left to the architects

involved. But the costs are now beginning to run high. In Toronto airport $150,000 was paid, I believe, for artistic objects of, to say the least, a controversial nature, and I am wondering whether in future it might not be a good idea to have these things checked by a government committee, perhaps including somebody from the national gallery. I say this because $150,000 is a sizeable chunk of the taxpayers' money, especially when it comes to the purchase of objects which are highly controversial even in artistic circles. One was described by a prominent Toronto artist as resembling a lump of mud. I think a little greater care should be exercised, and it might be a good idea to select objects which made concessions, at least to some extent, to the taste of the general public. Art galleries are perhaps another thing, but in the public airports one has to use a little reason.
It has been the fashion in the last few years to have large quantities of tropical plants scattered about our airports. These plants have an unfortunate habit of not living very long, and they are expensive to replace. This increases the cost of maintenance. All this may seem trivial, but I suggest that those responsible for the interior decor of airports and other government buildings might take a second look at the use of enormous quantities of tropical plants and devise some suitable alternative which would have a greater degree of permanence. I suggest some direct control be exercised by the department.

There is one further matter I wish to raise with the minister. The Yukon legislative council communicated with the hon. gentleman or his officials requesting that a member of the Department of Transport should travel to the Yukon and discuss with the council the requirement for terminal buildings, emergency airstrips and all the facilities needed in the Yukon. I am informed that the department refused to acknowledge this request. A similar request to the Department of Labour was, I understand, no more successful; there was no reply.
It seems to me that when a request comes from such a body as the Yukon legislative council the courtesy of expert advice and assistance should be extended to them if they request it in order to obtain the efficient service which they feel is required in the way of improved airstrips and facilities throughout the region.
I showed the minister a telegram I received the other day concerning the positioning of the terminal building at Whitehorse. Apparently it is to be placed in such a position that a discontinuance of the cross strip, the east-west runway, will be required. Great concern
Supply-Transport
is being expressed over this situation. I believe this question, along with others, could be solved if the minister would ask one of his officials to go and sit with the council as the council has requested.

I want to return to this question of Transair for a moment. Since the discussion has gone thus far, I think I should point out to the minister that there are many people along this southern prairie route who are deeply distressed because of the events which have taken place since last year. On December 11 of this year I put on the order paper a notice of motion for the production of papers asking for all correspondence between Transair and Trans-Canada Air Lines that would in fact reveal to members of the House of Commons what the arrangement or deal was.
I think the minister has taken the position that this is not public information but is an arrangement which was made between two companies. But as has been pointed out by hon. members just a few minutes ago, Transair knew very well when it undertook to provide this service that it was not going to pay, particularly on the basis they set it up. The results of the service for the few months they did carry it on substantiate that, of course, in that on one part of the run the number of passengers averaged .8 per trip. We do not disagree that this kind of service needs to be discontinued, but we are a little bit concerned about the position of competitors who may have been able to set up a service with schedules and so on that would have resulted in the service paying.
Transair also claims it lost a lot of money. No one can disagree with that if the figures they have given are true, and I am not disputing them. But we are going to pursue this matter in the next session because we want to know whether Trans-Canada did in fact transfer to Transair assets with a value in excess of the amount of money Transair lost. It may be a million dollars, it may be half a million dollars; apparently it is somewhere in that neighbourhood.
Transair operated this service for 117 days, I believe, and claim they lost up to $1,000 a day. If this is so it means that Transair got by way of assets from Trans-Canada Air Lines at least five or six times as much as Transair lost on the run. In my opinion, Mr. Chairman, this is wrong. I also believe that inasmuch as Trans-Canada Air Lines belongs to the people of Canada the House of Commons has a right to investigate this matter and also to have the answers from the minister; because it seems obvious to us that unless Transair knew in advance of the deal what assets Trans-Canada was prepared to transfer to

Supply-Transport
them for $1, they would never have undertaken to provide the service at all.
In spite of what the minister has said about not being able to get hold of the information that passed between Trans-Canada Air Lines and Transair, I believe that we as members of the house have a right to know if something like $300,000 to $500,000 in publicly owned assets were turned over to this corporation, which was then allowed to suspend the service.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Lapointe.
There are two points raised in the discussions, it seems to me-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Perhaps we could allow the Minister of Transport to reply to the points raised by previous speakers, and then I will recognize the hon. member for Lapointe.

It seems to me that there are two points involved in the remarks of the hon. member for Medicine Hat and to some extent in the earlier remarks of the hon. member for Port Arthur. I believe the point having to do with routes is fully answered by the fact that a hearing is going to be held. I would want to check my information, but I believe that already two applications have been made to serve parts of this route.
This is the very thing that should be determined by the air transport board, because it is a matter of examining the areas requiring service to see how they can best be served and what is the best method of getting some kind of service that will be effective. Obviously, as I think the hon. member realizes, a basis of service cannot be provided with an average of less than one passenger per flight, as was the case between a couple of points on that route. As to that part of the matter, I think the answer is surely satisfactory.

Before the minister leaves that point may I ask a question. Would the air transport board have any power to make Transair disgorge part of the planes and equipment it got to operate this route so they could be used to subsidize the successful applicant for the new franchise?

The question the transport board determined was whether or not they would permit them to cancel the service. As to the question put by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, I would think the answer would be that this was a commercial transaction between two air lines and that the board would not have any jurisdiction to inquire into it. But if the hon. member will bear with me until I deal with the other part

of the question raised by the other two members perhaps he will find his question sufficiently answered.
The transaction referred to was carried out under the former government before I had the responsibility of office. In the light of what has been said, in view of the motion for papers which was put on the order paper and possibly was withdrawn at my request- I do not know what became of it-and of the discussion that arose at that time, and in the light of repeated questions on this point by the hon. member for Port Arthur and the questions now raised by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, I am quite content as soon as the house finishes to have a look at the whole transaction to see if there is any ground on which I can with propriety produce information that would satisfy hon. members and show exactly the details of the whole situation. I shall make such an examination particularly with a view to seeing whether any part of this transaction falls within the realm of the government's responsibility and if the information thereon may be produced. But I do not want to recede from the position that information as to ordinary commercial transactions between air companies may not be produced, because it will be recognized that if I did that we would get into very serious situations. I will look at the whole matter in the light of the questions yesterday and today.

May I ask the minister another question before he sits down. I am not asking for details of the transaction between the two air companies, but I am asking the minister if Trans-Canada Air Lines, in giving Transair these planes and equipment, received any assurance that Transair would operate this route for any specific period of time.

Mr. Chairman, that is the very type of thing I have in mind. I want to examine the whole transaction in some detail, as is obviously required, and that is one of the many details that will have to be looked into. I must say I have not had any real opportunity to look at the matter at all in the past week since the matter was raised.

When the minister does come back to the house I would ask him to supply information so we will know the total fair value of all the planes and equipment involved and also the total loss of Transair while it operated the service, in order that we can make some comparisons and find out whether in fact they made a profit by losing money.

Mr. Chairman, I shall now turn to another matter with which the citizens of the Saguenay-Lake St. John area are very much concerned, the Bagotville airport.
Hon. members know that that airport is both a military and commercial airport. There have been accidents between T.C.A. aircraft and military aircraft using the landing strips there. The resulting danger makes the people in that area a little nervous, and they have requested for a long time a civil airport at St. Honore, near Chicoutimi, that is practically in the centre of the area.
I wonder whether the Minister of Transport contemplates setting up a civil airport at St. Honore.
Besides, the citizens of that area have been asking for some time for an air terminal in Bagotville, because there is, at present, a sort of building without any conveniences and with a waiting room totally out of date; it is necessary that conditions be improved. And, therefore, I ask the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mcllraith) whether he could give us some information regarding the building of a new airport or a new terminal in the Saguenay-Lake St. John area.
[Text}

I do not have much information on the precise details of the new airport. There are no immediate plans for it. However, in so far as the building to which the hon. member refers is concerned, I recall signing a letter on that subject within the last week. It is involved in the future plans, but I have forgotten the precise dates and the actual timing.
Will we have this new building for the airport in Bagotville without too long a delay?
I cannot tell my hon. friend anything offhand because I do not have the file. It depends on the estimates program; however I did deal with the new building within the past week.

Will the minister give us an up to date report on the status of the Malton airport? What is the stage of construction, and what is the estimated date for its official opening? There is a great deal of interest in this matter in Toronto.

I think the best information I can give the hon. member is that the airport will come into operational use at 12.01 a.m. on January 12, and that the formal opening will take place on February 28. I do not know that there is much I can usefully add to that.
I might take advantage of the opportunity to reply to a question asked by the hon.
Supply-Transport
member for Oxford. The answer is that the art selection is made by an art selection committee, one member of which is the head of the national gallery.

I should like to take a couple of minutes of the committee's time on one or two subjects. We have ranged rather far and wide, Mr. Chairman, so I hope you will let me conclude my remarks without interruption. First of all I should like to thank the minister for his co-operative attitude in connection with the representations I have made to him. We appreciate that.
However, I am a little concerned about airport facilities, particularly at Quesnel. The last time I was at Quesnel I saw the strange sight of the ticket agent making out tickets on the baggage wagon on the airstrip. There is absolutely no place in the Quesnel airport for passengers who are getting on or off planes. If it happens to be raining they have to get into a taxi or go into one of the hangar sheds for private aircraft. It would seem to me that one of the problems Canadian Pacific Airlines have in operating out of Quesnel is the lack of airport facilities for passengers.
Another thing that concerns me is the situation when an air service fails and for some reason or other cannot meet its scheduled flights. There have been cases where such a carrier had landing rights in certain airports and refused landing rights to other carriers who were willing to provide the service. I have actually had experience with this situation, and I hope a closer check will be made in connection with this matter so that people who want to get from one place to another when the regular carrier is unable to fulfil its obligations will have the right to use another carrier which is willing to provide the service. This is most important in an area such as the Cariboo, where there are a lot of air minded people. As the minister knows there are many aircraft being used, both private and commercial, because this particular area lends itself very well to air transport.
I believe that at the moment the fares on Canadian Pacific Airlines in this area are too high, and therefore they are not getting the traffic that is available. If the fares were reduced by even a small amount I am sure the traffic would increase and these large aircraft they are using would be filled closer to capacity. Perhaps the minister could use his influence in that regard, and I hope consideration will be given to this point.
I think it has been demonstrated by Pacific Western Air Lines that what they call a bus service between Edmonton and Calgary is practical. I think an air bus service from Whitehorse or from Fort St. John, with a

Supply-Transport
reduced fare and no reservations but just picking up your tickets on the aircraft, could provide better service all around.
There is one other thing I should like to mention, but I hesitate to do so. I hope when the minister goes to Winnipeg he does not have to shave with an electric razor. The washroom in Winnipeg, which is as big as any office in this building, has no outlet in which to plug an electric razor. I looked all over this new airport to find a place to use an electric razor and finally wound up in the kitchen. I hope the minister will have better success in finding the outlet than I did.

Mr. Chairman, I have a last question to put to the Minister of Transport. In view of the scope afforded by this item, the last one on that subject, can the Minister of Transport tell us whether it is true that when the contract was passed between T.C.A. and Douglas Aircraft in the United States, it was agreed that the tail units of the DC-9s would be built in Toronto and that the overhaul and maintenance of these aircraft would also be done at the Toronto plant?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. It seems the the question of the hon. member for Lapointe is in no way related to item 155. However, if the minister is willing to answer, he is free to do so. But the hon. member for Lapointe-
Mr. Chairman, I believe we are still on item 145.
No, we are now on item 155.
Mr. Chairman, I was under the impression that we were still considering item 145.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: No, we are now on item 155.
Mr. Chairman, as soon as you called the first item, if you remember, I rose and-
No, no, we are on item 155.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must tell the hon. member for Lapointe that item 145 was passed by the committee and that we are now discussing item 155.
Mr. Chairman, something is wrong here. If the item was passed, an hon. member was on his feet then.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member for Lapointe seems to forget that he has already spoken on item 145 which was passed later on.

Mr. Chairman, I do not know exactly what happened but there is a mistake. At any rate, I should like to have a reply to my question. I asked whether the contract

for the overhaul and maintenance of the DC-9 has been awarded to de Havilland.

The commercial contract is not before us, but in any event this question was answered in the committee, and it was proposed to do this work at the existing overhaul and maintenance base. Since that time another delegation has come with other ideas.

Mr. Chairman, I do not think
this question has been settled and that the committee has received an answer to it. A rather important principle is involved, owing to the fact that Trans-Canada Air Lines equipped and organized a whole plant in Montreal for the general maintenance and repair of those aircraft. But now, because a contract was passed, Montreal is to be deprived once again of the general maintenance and repair of the DC-9.
I feel a very important matter of principle is involved here, especially in view of the fact that expenditures were incurred for the repair of those jet aircraft at the base in Montreal. Moreover, since the DC-9 is being bought, all those expenditures will again be incurred in Toronto for the maintenance and repair of that aircraft. Now, that means that Montreal loses not only the contract for manufacturing part of this DC-9 aircraft, but also the maintenance and repair contract.

I am sorry to say the hon. member seems to have got a lot of very serious misinformation. Nothing is being taken away from Montreal, and that is the whole thing I am being attacked for these days. The overhaul for these aircraft has always been proposed for Montreal and there was no suggestion it be done in Toronto. As to the other part of the question, it has been stated in evidence many times that the Canadian share of the aircraft production is very high.

If I have been misinformed it was by a member of the cabinet, because on a motion for the production of documents the Minister of Industry said that the overhaul of these DC-9 aircraft would be done in Toronto, according to the contract between de Havilland and T.C.A. I would like to have the truth.

Perhaps I could give a short answer. The hon. member has misunderstood the whole matter as it affects overhaul and maintenance. The overhaul and maintenance by T.C.A. was proposed to be done in Montreal, subject only to the requests from other parts of the country that it be done

elsewhere. There has been no change in that whatsoever; but where the confusion is creeping in is that the hon. member is not aware of the nature of the work being done by the manufacturers of the aircraft at the de Havill-and plant in Toronto. It is true that certain company work is being done which is an obligation on the manufacturing company in Toronto. He is confusing that work with the work of the air line that buys these aircraft.

The confusion is due to the fact that we were told by the Minister of Industry that these aircraft would be overhauled and repaired in Toronto, according to the contract. I have had previous experience of this kind, when the Department of National Defence bought Voodoo aircraft from the United States, and it was a condition of the contract that for two years all the parts for those aircraft would be repaired in the factory in the United States. If that is the case with the DC-9, then they will be repaired in Toronto.

It is quite clear now that the overhaul the hon. member is speaking of concerns that work which is an obligation on the manufacturer, and that will be done in the de Havilland plant. This is a very good contract for Canada, but it has nothing to do with the points raised about the overhaul and maintenance by T.C.A., which will be done in Montreal.
Will the minister assure me that he will send an official of his department to confer with the legislative council of the Yukon?

I am sorry the question did not get answered, but I think there is a little misunderstanding about the facts. The department always sends officials out, and I believe a letter was sent within the last week on this subject. It has gone to some inquiring person or agency, with a view to having the appropriate persons sent from the department.

I know the letter has gone out because I have a copy of it, but it said that the department would not send any one to confer with the government of the Yukon. I would like to have the minister's assurance that he will have one of the officials comply with the request of the council.
My understanding of the letter is quite different from that. I will look into the matter again, but I understand the letter first asked for certain types of information.

Will the minister send an official?

I will look into the whole matter.

I would like to ask the minister if he could tell us something about the new chairman of the air transport board. Not too long ago the Canada Gazette announced the appointment of Mr. F. T. Wood of the city of Montreal, Quebec, to be a member for a term of ten years. I do not suggest that the minister give us the date of his birthday, as he did earlier this morning with regard to another appointment, but I would be interested to know some of the qualifications of Mr. Wood for this appointment. Perhaps the minister could also give us an explanation of the resignation of the former chairman of the board and what changes in board policy, if any, may be anticipated as a result of the appointment of Mr. Wood as the new chairman.

Mr. Chairman, I cannot give a long answer since I have no notes. Mr. Wood has been in the transport business all his life. He was first a Canadian National Railways employee and later joined Trans-Canada Air Lines, and became one of its vice presidents. He has been president of the air industries and transport association and is still a member of that board. He has had a great deal of experience in dealing with the relationships of air lines in the international field; that is, with air organizations and the negotiating end of air operations, both nationally and internationally. I do not know that there is much more I can usefully add.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask the minister, further, whether he can give any report on what consideration may be given to the suggestion that there be developed an arrangement of regional representation for the air transport board. I am wondering whether he may be willing to

Supply-Transport
consider the idea of setting up regional panels within the air transport board, which might involve some expansion of the membership of the board but on the other hand might enable the board to give more detailed consideration and attention to on the spot investigation of problems on a regional basis than has hitherto been the case.

Mr. Chairman, this question has received some consideration. I came to the conclusion that the best thing to do was continue with the three man board; that the way to meet the problem raised by he hon. member for Comox-Alberni is not by enlarging the board but by perfecting the board's hearings system, particularly with a view to regional hearings and that sort of thing. I think the hon. member will be interested to know that hearings will be taking place in his part of the country in the latter part of February.

I have one other matter that I would like to raise in connection with the operations of the air transport board. It has to do in particular with its terms of reference as drafted under the Aeronautics Act. I was interested earlier in the session to note that the minister was introducing a bill to amend the Aeronautics Act; but I was rather disappointed, when the bill came before the house and we were acquainted with its terms, that it made no reference to the particular area of the act in which I had become interested and about which I must confess I have some concern.
I think this might be a very appropriate time for me to bring forward a suggestion for the consideration of the minister. I suggest there is to be an amendment to the act. If my understanding is correct, the present bill is not likely to be dealt with prior to the end of this session. In the interval of time which will elapse between the end of this session and the beginning of the next the minister might be willing to agree to some redrafting of the present bill which would include this point.
My concern arises out of the present terms of the act in respect to appeals to the minister from decisions of the air transport board. I have a file here on the subject of disagreement with certain decisions of the board. It contains copies of a large number of petitions addressed to the minister in connection with the ruling of the board contained in decision No. 1865. I am not going to attempt at this time to go all through this file in discussing this question with the minister, but I am sure he will recall something of its contents. I will say, Mr. Chairman, for the information of the committee, that I do not recall any single

matter ever creating such a volume of communications from Comox-Alberni as did this particular decision of the air transport board. I think the committee will therefore readily understand my concern in the matter and my interest which led me to look at the Aeronautics Act in a way that I had not had occasion to do before.
The particular point about which I am quite concerned is this. As I understand the act, under section 15 (9) an air line which has made an application to the board for a certain form of licence has the right of appeal to the minister if it is dissatisfied with the decision of the board. But another air line which may consider itself adversely affected by the decision of the board, which air line was not an applicant, has not this right of appeal. Under the circumstances it would mean that in effect a decision of the board could put a competing air line out of business in favour of the applicant air line and they would have no right of appeal whatsoever. There was an attempt to appeal to the minister by one of the air lines involved in this situation. That appeal was disallowed by the minister on the technical ground that he had no jurisdiction, under the terms of the Aeronautics Act, to deal with their appeal.
This appears to me a rather inequitable state of affairs. I believe the Aeronautics Act should be amended in this connection so that any air line which considers that its vital interests have been adversely affected can have a review made of the matter. All air lines should be placed on an equal footing in this connection as far as the Aeronautics Act is concerned.
I am also rather concerned with the situation that arises under section 15 (10), which gives the air transport board the authority to alter or change or amend the conditions of the application in its original form. The result of the operation of this section is that when the board does use the authority-and I am given to understand that it is an authority which the board has rather seldom used-a form of licence can be granted which in effect is different from that which was notified to the interested parties prior to the hearings of the board.
I think the minister will recall that one or two of the air lines operating in my area felt themselves to be quite seriously aggrieved, and a great deal of the objection that arose on the part of the public and local organizations stemmed from the fact that they felt the board had made a decision with regard to which there had been no prior notice of hearings.
I would urge the minister to pay serious attention to these two subsections and consider an amendment to the Aeronautics Act

in this respect. I would certainly be interested to have some comment from the minister as to what consideration he is prepared to give to my argument, perhaps more particularly in respect of the question I have raised about the inequity of section 15 (9).

Mr. Chairman, I am familiar with the case the hon. member has raised and with the difficulty in the language used in the particular section to which he referred. I will have a look at his argument today to see how the problem can best be dealt with. The Aeronautics Act will be coming back for debate very early I hope in the new session, and there will then be an opportunity for an appropriate amendment to cover the point raised by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni if, after examination, he should find it advisable to do so. However, I will look at this matter in light of his arguments this morning as well as in light of some other rather technical legal arguments which have been raised subsequent to the decision to which the hon. member refers.

Mr. Chairman, I appreciate that this is a rather complicated matter and one of which I certainly do not claim to have any expert knowledge. But it seems to be that there is a prima facie case of inequity in the way the present clause 9 reads.

Then I will take advantage of vote 212 to raise a matter that is of great importance to the people of southeastern British Columbia, and I make no apology for this final appeal because time is of the essence. The governor in council is required to make a decision by January 16 with respect to the termination of passenger service on the Kettle Valley railway. I have been asked to bring this matter to the attention of the committee by residents of Fernie, Kimberley, Nelson, Trail and Penticton. For some years we have been suffering from a limited and split passenger service on this very important railway, a decision initiated in the first instance owing to supposed danger from bombing attacks by the Sons of Freedom. That matter has now been overcome so it is no longer a consideration.
Some time ago the Canadian Pacific Railway made application to the board of transport commissioners to discontinue this passenger service, and hearings were held in the district. So was the city of Cranbrook and the Cranbrook chamber of commerce; the brotherhood of locomotive engineers; the brotherhood of railroad trainmen; the city of Lethbridge; the village of Natal; the Nelson chamber of commerce and the city of Nelson; local 480 of the international union of mine, mill and smelter workers; Tye; and also the Kootenay lake bible camp and others.

I have received telegrams from Nelson, Trail and Rossland, and I have handed them over to the minister. A good number of these municipalities and other organizations are sending petitions to the governor in council because of the changed circumstances.
Just to indicate the thinking of the people of the district I am going to read one petition sent by the Nelson chamber of commerce:
Petition: We the Nelson chamber of commerce hereby humbly pray to appeal against the ruling

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this matter raised by the hon. member for Kootenay West is of very great importance to the entire southeastern portion of British Columbia, as a matter of fact to the entire southern portion of the province outside of the lower mainland. The minister will tell the hon. member that I have brought this matter both to his attention and to that of the government on a number of occasions, and the minister has assured me that as soon as the session is over and the work load becomes a little less arduous he will be considering the question of the board's order to allow the C.P.R. to withdraw this service.
It might be well to mention here, Mr. Chairman, that one of the most lucrative subsidiaries of the Canada Pacific Railway, and I believe one of the subsidiaries that makes the greatest contribution to the dividends paid by the railway company, is itself located in this area. That is the huge smelter mentioned by the hon. member, the mines in Kimberley

adjacent to Cranbrook and, of course, the vast fertilizer industry established by the same company in Trail.
Unquestionably this service is losing money for the railway company. The submission to the board indicated, I believe, that the company is losing some $500,000 as a result of so few passengers using the service. The service consists of Budd cars, units which can be operated relatively cheaply, yet the operation has been showing a deficit of $500,000 when all costs have been considered.
Should this service be discontinued $500,000 of the taxpayers' money would be saved. This is axiomatic when one considers that we are now subsidizing the railways to the extent of $70 million on a straight grant basis to provide additional revenue to the companies because they have not been allowed to increase their rates as permitted by the board. I suggest that the Department of Transport consider spending an equal amount of money in providing safe all weather airstrips which would enable us to have the benefit of a first class air service in that area at all times. The hon. member for Kootenay West has told the committee that the air service in this area is not dependable in the winter months and I think we can realize why, when we consider that the airport of which he was speaking is situated between two high mountain ranges. The hon. member for Yukon can talk about airstrips running east and west and the danger of having them obstructed by terminals. In the area of which I am speaking we have our strips running in one direction only because that is the only direction which they can run, in other words parallel to the mountain ranges.
There are these difficulties about providing a service, but I wish to say that Canadian Pacific has provided an excellent service having regard to all these circumstances. If Mr. McConachie were required to come before a house committee, as is Mr. McGregor of T.C.A., to report on the activities of his company I think we would find that this air route has been operating since 1946 and showing a deficit during all those years. The company is attempting to provide a good service, and I am sure if the department were to make better landing facilities available we would see a great improvement in the service during the winter months.
The railway service is an old and historic service and its discontinuance would represent a serious backward step. I ask the minister now publicly to give this matter serious consideration as soon as the house prorogues, sometime this afternoon.

Mr. Chairman, since that subsidy will be granted again, I wish to say a few words about it.
First, I want to point out to the house that those payments or subsidies are granted to all railways, which use them to reduce their freight rates. That being so, the railways are competing unfairly with the trucking companies because the federal government grants subsidies to the railways on a percentage of the cost of transport, whereas the truckers do not get the same advantages.
I wish to point out to the minister that the subsidies amounting to $50 million, which are given to the railways only and not to the air transport companies or the trucking companies, are taken out of the taxes paid by the people and the Canadian corporations.
Trucking companies and truckers pay taxes which are used to grant subsidies to railway companies, thus letting them compete with their own enterprises.
Mr. Chairman, you will agree with me that this does not make sense. Why tax private enterprise so as to make it possible for public enterprise to compete with it.
It should be noted that the C.N.R., for instance, does not pay any taxes; but it is the money collected from the truckers which will help the C.N.R. and the C.P.R. to compete with them in the transportation field.
I think that this is illogical, unfair and illegal competition on the part of a crown corporation and against private companies.
At the meeting of the sessional committee on railways, I asked the president of the Canadian National Railways, Mr. Donald Gordon, whether he would agree to the granting of this subsidy not only to the railways but to all freight carriers. The president of the Canadian National Railways replied that he would readily agree to the granting of these subsidies not only to the railways but to trucking companies as well.
It seems to me then that, if it were so, competition would be fair and that there would not be this attempt to drive the trucking industry to bankruptcy. That would be only fair for all transport companies, including trucking and air transport companies.
I wonder if the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mcllraith) would agree with the trucking companies which made representations and with the president of the Canadian National Railways, so that those subsidies be granted not

only to the railways but to all carriers including trucking and air transport companies.
I ask the minister if he is prepared to change those payments in order to grant them to all transport companies operating in Canada.

Mr. Chairman, just before the minister rises to answer I should like to express my support of what the hon. member has said about this matter, because it seems to me that under the present set-up we are in fact using public funds to direct business to the railroads in a discriminatory manner, and we do not allow the same thing to happen with private firms. If we are going to have these subsidies I believe that the trucking firms should have an equal opportunity, so that at point of origin freight can be designated to go either by truck or rail. I certainly feel that a choice is not given shippers in this matter because of this situation.
The minister knows, of course, that the matter was discussed to quite an extent in the committee. When this question does come up for final consideration I hope we will put an end to this type of thing and bring things out into the open so that truckers can compete with the railways on a fair basis. As far as I am concerned the trucker is not given a fair shot at the business at all.
On this particular point I should like the minister to clear up a question in my mind. So far as the railways are concerned, do they receive this subsidy on any goods that they move by truck?

The answer to that question is no. The essential difference between the trucking industry and the railways has been completely missed in the discussion of this item. This item was provided for the railways by the former government because the railways were prevented from adjusting their freight rates. In order to compensate them for the arbitrary restriction of their right to adjust their freight rates, this payment was provided. I am somewhat amazed to hear hon. members who come from areas where great quantities of freight originate that require to be shipped by rail raising any question at all about this item.
In any event, the truckers are free to charge whatever rates they like, and so far the government has not seen fit to restrict the rates they can charge. The whole premise on which the argument of the hon. member for Lapointe was based disappears. The item is one that I hope will disappear in this form from the estimates. It really is an item that arises because of the delay in dealing with the railway legislation based upon the Mac-Pherson royal commission report. I must say
[Mr. Gregoire.l
I am rather disappointed that there was no opportunity to deal with that legislation at this session, because it is a piece of legislation that I think is of vital significance and of some urgency to the country.

Mr. Chairman, if we ever heard a specious argument, it is the one that has just been advanced by the Minister of Transport, when he said that the government does not control trucking rates as it does for the railways.
It is obvious that the government, by trying to restrict freight rates, wanted to cope with a substantial increase in freight rates. But to correct one evil, it produced another one which it does not seem ready to remedy. To grant subsidies to railway companies in order to prevent an increase in their rates is like saying that since railway companies have now a given rate, trucking companies that want to remain competitive with them are compelled to maintain their own rates at a relatively low level.
It is obvious that the government does not and cannot control private trucking companies' rates. But if special subsidies are paid to the railways so that they can maintain their rates at a relatively low level, trucking companies have to do the same, and this represents an indirect way of controlling the rates of the said companies. However, as truckers do not get special subsidies from the government, they have to put up with losses if they want to maintain their rates at the same level as the railways'; and if their rates are higher than those of the railways, they are not competitive and the shippers use the railways. It is therefore by means of the government's subsidies that the railways enter into unfair competition with the trucking companies.
The government controls the trucking rates, if not directly, at least indirectly, as these rates are compulsory for the trucking companies that wish to remain competitive not only as regards the C.N.R. but railway companies operating in Canada.
That is why we suggest to the Minister of Transport that the legislation should be changed. As I said a moment ago, although the subsidies were granted to prevent an exorbitant increase in rates, I am afraid that by trying to cure one ill, the government has brought about another one: the unfair, illogical and illegal competition of railway companies against private trucking companies.
That is why I ask the minister to enlighten the house about the government plans on that point for the coming year. Is it the

minister's intention to put the railway companies on an equal footing with the trucking and air line companies? What are the solutions that he could propose before too long to solve that problem?
I would like to hear the answer of the Minister of Transport.

Before the minister speaks, if he does answer, I should like to say that I do not want to be misunderstood. The minister said he was surprised that the question was raised in connection with a possible reduction of freight rates to consumers. We are not against that, and we do not want to be misunderstood. What I am saying is that the shipper has no choice in placing an order because of the 9 per cent difference between the truckers' rate and the railway rate which results from this subsidy.

Mr. Chairman, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Megantic (Mr. Langlois):
That item 213a be not voted in its present form, but that it be granted for any type of transportation, of the shipper's choice.

I realize that since these estimates were discussed on a previous occasion the Secretary of State for External Affairs has visited NATO headquarters; and while most of us realize that no great, momentous decisions were made at NATO, because of the newness of various heads of states for other reasons, nevertheless I wonder if he, in his customary genial manner, could attempt to give us some information on what went on at the NATO meeting. I would also like to have his comments, briefly, on the likelihood of Canada securing a seat on the security council of the United Nations.
This is a matter which I have raised on various occasions, and in the interval between [The Deputy Chairman.]
the minister's attendance at the NATO meeting in Paris it has gained a great deal of prominence at the United Nations. As hon. members know, the Soviet union has made it quite clear the security council will not be expanded until such time as the People's Republic of China is given the Chinese seat. As a result the available non-permanent seats are going to have to be redistributed to provide for Asian and African representation.
In all likelihood the commonwealth seat will have to go, if it has not already gone. The other day the Prime Minister was a little clearer in the house on this question than the Secretary of State for External Affairs had been, but he pointed out-and I am fully aware of them-the difficulties which the Secretary of State for External Affairs has in this problem. There is no easy answer to it, but if the commonwealth seat goes at the next meeting of the general assembly and is filled by an Asian or African member, then Canada will be left with no place to go. In other words she will have no group to join in order to obtain a seat on the security council, and I think everybody would agree that would be a ridiculous situation in view of the work and the assistance which Canada has supplied to the United Nations.
There are two alternatives. Canada could go with the Latin American group or the west European group, but that would only give her a chance to secure a seat on the council every ten or 12 years, and this would not be very suitable. The other possibility, which I have mentioned on previous occasions and which I would like to draw to the minister's attention again, is that if the redistribution takes place a number of other countries will be in the same position as Canada, countries like Australia, New Zealand, Israel, Cyprus and perhaps the two West Indian countries, Jamaica and Trinidad. Although I hope every effort will be made to retain the commonwealth seat, possibly some arrangement could be made in the interim, until the security council is expanded, whereby the countries I have mentioned could form a group in order to obtain a one year seat on the security council. Canada, Australia and New Zealand are three charter members of the United Nations and have contributed to it in a great many ways. I have a feeling that if the minister went out and really tried to sell this proposition among the other countries in the United Nations he might have the same success he had in days gone by when he introduced the package deal providing membership for all the new countries in the United Nations.
I am concerned about Australia and New Zealand but more concerned about what will happen to Canada, because our role at the

United Nations has been such that I am sure nearly every member country would agree we are entitled to have an opportunity to serve on the security council and the other councils of the organization.

Mr. Chairman, there was an ancient Greek philosopher called Heraclitus who said you cannot stand in the same stream twice; everything is in flux; everything is in change. I believe we should take a look at our attitude toward NATO, the commonwealth, the United Nations and at our associations with Britain and the United States, which are always in a state of change. Today our relationship with Britain has matured, but our association with the United States is under critical review. The emergence of our southern neighbour as the political leader of the free world, and the most powerful of all the world's economies, has placed special stresses on our thinking, for we have profited much in terms of our security and economic growth by the easy relationship which ensued between us for more than a century.
It is important to separate in our minds the problems which are disturbing us. The role of the United States as leader of the western alliance should not be confused with the question of United States capital investment in Canadian development. We can only welcome the profitable participation of friends in our economic growth. Our ability to provide solutions that meet our national needs and prove attractive to foreign investors is our task, not theirs.
Trade problems also influence our relationship with the United States. Here there is a closer association between political and economic policy, and the United States must follow policies of trade which will give strength to her leadership and not frustrate it.
The pull of the frontier endowed American life with a spirit of optimism and a faith in the invincibility of American power. Much of this democracy has given a special and attractive quality to American society. It has also had its shortcomings, and among these have been the inward-looking tendency of American public life, its messianism, its boundless optimism, its refusal to plan because the realization of the American dream was inevitable in any case.
The role of the United States as a world leader was thrust upon her. There was to be a rude awakening. Today we still live with the shock of Pearl Harbor. The United States has learned that it must play a large role and that the price of leadership is not always sweet. The American public has learned that to meet the challenges of the
Supply-External Affairs 1960's it does not possess resources without limit. The United States also needs allies, and it prizes them.
The death of John Kennedy removed a powerful leader who was not the product of a disenchantment with the American tradition, but the eloquent spokesman of a new and mature pragmatism that has been willing to accept the burdens of its role and looks to its allies to accept theirs. It would be unworthy for Canadians to be anti-American as it has been unworthy for Canadians to be anti-British or anti-French. The passions that were expressed about Britain between the two wars have subsided not only because Britain is different, but because we too have changed. But the lesson remains. As a member of a wider alliance we must press for what we think is right, while remaining loyal to our allies and associates.
John Kennedy was not a typical American in a society where the collective pressures to conform are so powerful. His love of learning for the sake of learning marked him as someone special. His refusal to bow to the orgy of sentimentalism that on occasion engulfs his people marked him as a strong individualist. His personal dignity and that of his wife have shown them as chief citizens who eschewed the popular humdrum. His belief in the equality of man before the law, as expressed by the highest tribunal in his land, will remain his finest hour as it is the blessing of the American commonwealth.
To play our part we must strengthen our own national life for the benefit of all Canadians. The economic growth of our country provides us the sinews for international policy. We must be wise, and we must have the wherewithal to underwrite our judgment. We must have amity. In our broad country there is scope for all who live here. If we are to be torn by a struggle between our two chief cultural groups, then we will have less to say, we will have less for each to do. A frantic dialogue can enervate our national being and frustrate the well-intentioned purposes of all. Abroad, we could only sink in the scale of those who are contributing to peace and well-being. The first test of our statesmanship is leadership at home. This means both national and provincial and in the area of all those voluntary groups which contribute so much to our national life.
In working for a world at peace we seek the extension of the rule of law. We were among the founding members of the United Nations and have joined each of its specialized agencies. Through the developing commonwealth and in association with our NATO

Supply-External Affairs allies we are daily seeking to strengthen the forces of peace and to make more abundant the avenues of international well-being.
Canadians must be prepared to share office with more members in the committees of the United Nations and in its secretariat. Canada's influence now more especially will be related to the wisdom of its counsel and the strength of its national life at home. The shifting emphases in NATO reflect in part the recovery of Europe itself, which NATO was formed to protect. The underpinning of European peace was recognized as the special interest of all the partners, and the English speaking members made commitments stronger, more pervasive and automatic than ever before, which marked a turning point in the history of the west. To resist the encroachments of Soviet power was sworn on the headstone of Czech democracy.
The discomfitures in NATO arise not alone from jealousies over sovereign power, but the very sinews of national being are at stake in the problems of industrial production, of markets and the race for nuclear technology. These problems of Europe and the Atlantic community pose difficult challenges to American leadership of the west, to the European members themselves, and to countries like Canada which have an important interest and must have an opinion about these serious issues.
We all welcome the moves which the government has made to increase Canadian participation in programs of aid to underdeveloped countries. This was first marked by doubling the allotment to the special United Nations fund. In his recent statement the Secretary of State for External Affairs outlined government policy for an additional $70 million in the fiscal year 1964-65. These programs which assist the developing countries to help themselves are a growing aspect of our foreign policy. Foreign aid will remain a facet of our public life during the lifetime of all members of this house, and beyond. We must cast it in these terms, and international assistance will grow as an aspect of our national policy. It seems to me that we should continue to support all those multilateral programs which have grown under the aegis of the United Nations and have to their credit many brilliant accomplishments. The devotion and service of peoples from diverse backgrounds who have contributed in a spirit of dedication places us in their debt. Among these are many splendid Canadians.
While we view foreign aid as a permanent feature of our public life, we must plan our programs in terms of our over-all economic policies. Here is the union of the right and of national interest, and we must be ashamed of neither. Foreign aid, like all economic

programs, must be viewed as part of our own economic growth and part of the important objective of full employment for Canadians. To further these aims and to give greater weight to foreign assistance programs, it seems to me that we are going to have to expand our bilateral programs. These provide the more likely avenues for a wide expansion of this special international activity.
There is another facet which we must not neglect. I mentioned the Canadians who have given service abroad. In most of the developing countries there is a lack of knowhow. The skills we have, we can share. The programs of investing in the skills of our people should be related to needs both at home and abroad. Many Europeans have given this service when the flags of their motherlands flew over the lands of colonial peoples often rich in great traditions but poor in the techniques needed to help themselves. Canada should provide career opportunities for those who wish to serve abroad. It was suggested by the former secretary general of the United Nations, the late Dag Hammars-kjold, that the United Nations itself should create such an international agency through which people of skill could be seconded to developing countries seeking to borrow special talents. The agency could provide the security and the career opportunities which a recipient country is unable to offer. Canada itself could start such a program through a special section of the civil service. Men and women specially recruited and trained could thus bring their talents to the international scene where such avenues are now provided in modest measure.
In a world of turmoil we are jealous of fundamental rights and liberties of all human beings. The United Nations, through its commission on human rights, has provided an important means for the discussion of these important issues. The position of Jewish people in the Soviet union is a case in point. This is one aspect of Stalin's policy which Khrushchev has not neglected, although the means are different. The Soviet union is based on the legal recognition of nationalities and, within the context of this law, Jews are designated as a nationality. Jews constitute slightly more than 1 per cent of the Soviet population and are eleventh among the nationalities. Thirty eight per cent live in the Russian republic, 37 per cent in the Ukraine and 7 per cent in white Russia. In a country where they have resided for over a thousand years they are looked upon as an alien group. Policy toward the Jews and Judaism has remained the same since 1948. The communist poet Yevtushenko asked why there was no monument to the thousands of Jews slaughtered by the nazis outside Kiev, at Babi

Yar. There is a strong tradition of antiSemitism in Russia, in which the Soviet leaders have been raised. But there have also been other voices. No Hebrew bible has been published since 1917. Not a single Jewish religious book has appeared since 1920. Synagogues have been closed; the study of Hebrew forbidden; Jewish religious observances hounded and harried. This process has been stepped up since the middle of 1961. The public baking of matzah-unleavened bread-for the Passover has been forbidden since the spring of 1962.
Attacks on Jews and Judaism have been published in the communist press. Elderly religious Jews have their names listed in the press, together with the names of their children, stating public positions and places of work. This is to hold them up to ridicule and is effective social blackmail. The economic crimes which have led to public trials are almost unbelievable, and death has been the frequent verdict. That within the context of a communist society another economy exists is like Alice in Wonderland. This is not even state capitalism. Karl Marx said in his attack on the rise of capitalism in England that when they stopped burning witches they started hanging men for stealing horses. The progress from Stalin to Khrushchev may be mirrored here.
Edward Crankshaw of the London Observer, as printed in the Globe and Mail of Saturday, November 16, reports a trial where the accused "contrived to perfect a racket which diverted a great deal of the products of no less than 52 state-owned factories and a number of collective farms into their own pockets". One "had bribed his way into a political post which put him in charge of a 'psycho-neurological health centre' where a large number of patients were innocently engaged in occupational therapy. By bribery and blackmail on a majestic scale, he and" another "turned this modest outfit into a commercial underwear factory, fitting it out with the latest machines embezzled from state-owned enterprises, diverting wool-460 tons in all-from collective farms, sent out the manufactured articles to be finished at other state-owned factories, and privately selling the final products in markets and at railway stations".
Of course the accused were trapped because an accomplice, who sold his wife to one of the plotters, confessed to the police, who found under the floor boards of their house rubles valued at $300,000, and bullion in gold bars. The picture was perfect. The Soviet union confesses that within a communist society exists a highly organized economy of the demi-monde, equipped with everything, even gold bars. The Soviet union is 28902-5-401
Supply-External Affairs loth to have meetings of the United Nations commission on human rights. Canada must be one of the guardians of this tribune of fundamental freedoms and ensure that it is not put aside.
The influence of Canada abroad can only be impaired by bitter struggles at home. Sparsely spread along the southern frontier of our great continental land mass, we have only emerged as a country of significance and a people of achievement because for two centuries we have lived and worked together on a basis of give and take. That tolerance is the mortar of our edifice. Should it not withstand the weathering of time, then surely what we have built will crumble.
To be a Canadian is to be proud of our achievement. Should we lose the sense of the worthwhileness of what we are doing we will never respect ourselves nor command the loyalty and allegiance of others with whom we are associated in the great tasks of building peace and well-being. We must stand for understanding both at home and abroad, and this we share with our friends and allies.
The eternal flame which was lit over the grave of Jack Kennedy in Arlington Park will pierce the darkness where prejudice abounds and provide a beacon to men who dream and struggle for freedom. This is something for us all.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I had the privilege, along with others, of being a member of the standing committee on external affairs, the sessions of which were very ably conducted by the hon. member for Leeds, assisted at times by the vice chairman, the hon. member for Queens. I am sure all of us who were members of that committee feel that even though it was late in starting-it had to meet at a time when there was competition for space, and so on-nevertheless its sessions were worth while, and we hope that at the next session this important committee will meet earlier.
It is not my intention to rehash any of the matters discussed by the committee on external affairs. Rather there are two subjects on which I wish to speak briefly. The first is one which has arisen since the committee held its sessions; the second is a matter part of which has just been referred to by the hon. member for York South.
