The reason I did not raise this before the committee is that the minister himself was not able to be there all the time, and the matter was such that I wanted to raise it when he was present.
The first matter, one which has come up since the sessions of the committee, is, I freely admit, a delicate one. Nevertheless I think it ought not to be delicate, and that the Secretary of State for External Affairs should

Supply-External Affairs comment upon it. It came up yesterday or last night during discussion of the estimates of the Department of Transport. I think it was somewhat out of order at that point, but it is certainly in order now. It arises, at least as far as I am aware, from an article which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press on Thursday of this week under the by-line of Victor Mackie. The headings are rather interesting. The article is headed "Diplomatic eyebrows up. Canada raps French critics. Federal government angered over embassy's too open pressing for Caravelle". I should like to read the first paragraph of Mr. Mackie's article which appears, as I say, in the Winnipeg Free Press of December 19, on page 1.
Activities of the French embassy in Ottawa during the period when the cabinet was considering Trans-Canada Air Lines' decision to purchase the DC-9 medium-range jet embarrassed members of the Canadian government, it was learned here today from informed sources.
The French government has been made aware of the embassy's unusual activities. It has been drawn to the French government's attention that their embassy in Canada appeared to capitalize on the delicate English-French situation within this country to promote the interests of the Caravelle.
I was quite interested in the comments made on this matter last night, and I recognize the motives behind those comments. I think it is pretty generally known that I am one of the strong advocates, of whom there are many of us in this house of all parties, of equal rights for the two main groups which make up this country of ours. But it seems to me we should not confuse the rights of the French language and the English language and the rights of the French culture and the English culture in Canada with an issue of this kind. It is my view that if it is true that the ambassador of a friendly country, the country of France, used his position in this country on behalf of a commercial outlet in his own country, and if he exploited a difficult situation which we had in this country, there is reason for these headlines; there is reason to believe that the federal government must at least have been embarrassed, if not angered, over what happened.
I express the hope that the minister, diplomatically but nevertheless clearly, will give us his view of this incident. At first when press reports appeared about this one wondered whether it was really true. Then reports seemed to mount. Yesterday morning there was a preview commentary on this matter over the C.B.C., although I think the speaker on that occasion did not refer to the embassy but to the French government participating in this matter. But last night the hon. member for Three Rivers, as far as he had knowledge of it, seemed to confirm that this actually took place and that the ambassador of France to this country did participate in the matter.

On occasion American officials in this country have done things which we did not like, and we have said so. I think we should continue to do so. Not long ago in a British Columbia election I think there was a complaint about a United States government representative in this country. I do not think our sensitivities on this question should keep us from bringing this incident out into the open too. I believe our diplomatic relations with friendly countries will be maintained in the way they ought to be maintained only if the proprieties of diplomatic relationships are respected.
I should like to hear from the Secretary of State for External Affairs on this matter. Does he have knowledge that these activities were carried on? Has the Canadian government made its views on this question known to the ambassador of France or, through our ambassador in Paris, to the French government? I noted what the Secretary of State said about the capacity of the Secretary of State for External Affairs for eloquent flights. However, even if he is to make an eloquent flight I hope he will not fail to speak to us diplomatically and calmly, but nevertheless clearly, on this issue.
It had been my intention a few minutes ago to make this small contribution to the debate and then to sit down and let the minister comment if he would, and then to rise later and raise the other issue. But because of the latter part of the remarks of the hon. member for York South I feel I should deal with this other question at this time. 1 for one was interested in the entire speech made by the hon. member for York South, even though it is the last day of the session, which is not usually a day when long speeches on philosophical and international issues are the order of the day. Nevertheless it was a good speech. I liked in particular his bringing out into the open another delicate question and one that concerns us, namely evidence of antiSemitic practices in the Soviet union. With what the hon. member for York South said I am in complete agreement. I think in all parts of the house there is agreement with and sympathy for the point of view he expressed.
I only wish he had gone a little further, and that he had told us what the present government's position is on this matter. I am sure that as a member of this house he must know of documents which have been tabled. He must know about the one I have in mind, because he was here when I asked for it to be tabled. I refer to sessional paper No. 264, tabled on Wednesday, November 27, 1963. This document consists in the main of a communication addressed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs by the Canadian Jewish Congress over the signature of Mr. DECEMBER 21, 1963
Michael Garber, the president of the congress. In addition to that letter there is a copy of the reply which the Secretary of State for External Affairs wrote to Mr. Garber's letter. Mr. Garber's letter was written on October 8, 1963 and the reply was written under date of October 30.
Mr. Garber in his letter referred to a portion of a brief presented earlier to the Prime Minister on behalf of the Canadian Jewish Congress, and both that portion of the brief and Mr. Garber's letter referred to the very things about which the hon. member for York South has told us. In particular there was a specific reference to a rabbi in the Soviet union who was charged with certain alleged economic malpractices, and there was a possibility at that time that this rabbi would be sentenced to the death penalty for those alleged practices.
It is hard to believe that this kind of thing can happen in our modern world. When it happened some years ago in an other country our consciences were shocked. They were even more shocked when it was over and we were aware of the extent of it. I remember being in this house when we considered these matters and passed certain legislation concerning them. I remember when we considered the universal declaration of human rights and when we discussed a convention against genocide, and I felt that the house was resolving in its heart, man by man, that we would never again countenance anything of that sort no matter where it reared its head.
I think the letter of Mr. Garber was restrained and reasonable. In the main it asked two things. It asked that the government take the matter up with the Soviet union through diplomatic channels; and second, that it raise the subject of discrimination and anti-Semitism in the Soviet union in the third committee of the general assembly of the United Nations. I do not intend to take up the time of the committee by reading Mr. Garber's letter. I hope hon. members will take my word that it is a well composed document, restrained in its requests. I feel it should have been responded to in a positive way.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs, when he replied, expressed concern, sympathy and understanding. He went on to say he doubted whether there was any official program encouraging anti-Semitism in the Soviet union but, nevertheless, it existed. In fact he used language almost the same as that which the hon. member for York South used a few minutes ago about the way it had been going on for hundreds of years with some of it, which is there now, being residual from what had been there in the past. But when the Secretary of State for External Affairs 28902-5-401i
Supply-External Affairs got to the two specific requests that the matter be taken up with the government of the Soviet union and raised in the third committee of the general assembly, this is what he had to say. In a lengthy paragraph he referred to the fact that the creation of the state of Israel had heightened suspicion of the Jewish community in the Soviet union. Then he said:
This suspicion continues, and it has been our policy, therefore, to avoid any action which would emphasize the Jews' foreign connections and confirm Soviet fears. We would be loath, therefore, to make representations directly from the Canadian government to the Soviet government on the rabbi's behalf as it would emphasize the foreign ties and might provoke a renewed drive against the Jews.
That is the response made to the specific request contained in the letter with regard to representations. As to the second request, that the subject be raised in the committee, I should like to read the following paragraph from the letter written by the Secretary of State for External Affairs:
Although the third committee at the United Nations will not be discussing the question of religious intolerance in any detail this year, the Canadian representative will at some point be making a statement on human rights. If an appropriate occasion arises, it might be possible to make reference in a general way to religious persecution in the Soviet union, which is not directed only against those of the Jewish faith. For the reasons outlined above, however, I would prefer that strictures on the practice of the Jewish religion not be mentioned specifically.
I can only hope the hon. member for York South has not read this letter, because I am sure he would have been scandalized by it. Or perhaps he has read the letter and has decided to ignore it.
If these practices exist at all we should not be so unwilling to mention the question to a friendly nation, bearing in mind that we belong to a generation which has memories of what anti-Semitism did not only to millions of Jews but also to the hearts and souls of all of us. We should not be so unwilling to raise a question on the subject of human rights at the United Nations. I asked for this document to be tabled at a time when a delegation of Canadians was seeking to meet officials of the Soviet embassy here in Ottawa. I know the people who were planning to meet them, and I know that up until the day they were hoping to go they had been given no assurance that they would even be allowed in the embassy. But they were allowed in and they did have a discussion, and I suggest this emphasizes a point which Mr. Garber made in his letter to the minister, namely that the detente we seem to be enjoying at the moment is an occasion when it might be possible to discuss some of these things and get somewhere with them.

Supply-External Affairs
Like other members of this house I have had the opportunity of visiting Berlin recently. I remember, when I saw the wall while we were there in September, it looked like something which would never be breached. Today many thousands of West Berliners are at least getting a day in East Berlin. The impossible can happen. I plead with the Secretary of State for External Affairs not to treat this as a subject which should not be raised. 1 ask him to listen to the eloquent words which were uttered on this subject by the hon. member for York South. I ask him to reconsider the letter he wrote to the Canadian Jewish Congress. I ask that Canada carry forward the sense of resolution we had with regard to this question during the second world war and immediately after when we said, in our hearts if we did not say it openly, that we would never again keep quiet in the face of antiSemitism anywhere in the world.
These are the two subjects I wished to raise. Neither of them was raised in the committee. I should like to hear from the minister, when we return after our half hour break. What does he think about these reports of the activities of the French embassy, and what has he to say about the government's responsibility to state Canada's position with regard to combating anti-Semitism anywhere in the world?
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 1.30 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to say a few words on this item rather than wait for the particular item, because I suppose we will be in a greater rush than ever then. I should have liked to say something about external affairs in general but I realize that time is limited. I was a member of the committee, but being a member of other committees also I unfortunately was not able to attend many sessions. I hope that next year our committees will start early in the session so we will only have a third of them sitting at a time and can really do the work that is required.
I have been sitting here almost restlessly, Mr. Chairman, expecting a statement from the Secretary of State for External Affairs on the negotiations with respect to the Columbia, but I assume we will hear from him at great length when I have concluded. I am going to confine my few brief remarks to a particular aspect of this matter, because it does provide an opportunity to advance one argument which I trust will have some effect on what up to now appears to be the

minister's impervious mind in this respect. I wish to refer to a motion I moved for the production of papers, and I really have a complaint here. On October 30 I moved, seconded by the hon. member for Port Arthur, and it was ordered:
That there be laid before this house a copy of all correspondence and telegrams exchanged between the Prime Minister, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources or their offices and any private citizen in Canada with respect to the Columbia river treaty since May 1, 1963.
I have risen on a few occasions, Mr. Chairman, to suggest that we were looking forward to the production of these papers. I mentioned it again today and the Prime Minister did not give a very satisfactory answer. I do hope these papers will be produced before this session ends, because they are interesting letters and there are a lot of people who are anxious to peruse them prior to the commencement of the new session. I do ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs to open his heart in this respect. I am told privately that the person who is really holding them up is the secretary of the privy council, Mr. Gordon Robertson. I am told he is primarily responsible for advising the minister not to release them.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is wholly inaccurate.

I am glad to hear that, because I could not understand why that would be done. In any event, I do urge that these papers be produced before this session ends, which I trust will be by midnight today.
I rise particularly to bring to the minister's attention the concern of the governments of the prairie provinces, organizations in the prairie provinces and many individuals with regard to the protection of water resources that will be required for future development on the prairies. There is a great deal of concern in that respect. The western reclamation association had a meeting last year in Vernon, and against the protests of Hon. Ray Wil-liston unanimously passed a resolution supporting General McNaughton's scheme on the Columbia because they know that in that scheme there would be provision for their water requirements.
In contrast to the attitude, as we understand it, of the government of Canada and the government of British Columbia, what do we find in the states to the south of British Columbia and Alberta? In that connection I want to quote briefly from an article in the Christian Science Monitor of December 7 last headed "Northwest Opposes Sharing of Water":

The Pacific northwest states of the Columbia basin-their future water supply more secure than that of any other region in the nation-will not gladly share that resource. Opposition has been general in Oregon, Washington and Idaho to a Los Angeles proposal that a 519 mile aqueduct be constructed to siphon off Pacific northwest water to the relief of parched southern California.
Consensus of official statements, newspaper editorials, and other expressions of opinion in the northwest has been:	Let people come to the
northwest if they want the northwest's prime resource-water.
What we say is, let people come to British Columbia if they want our power for industry. I mention that to indicate how concerned they are with preserving their water rights and not giving them away without certain requirements of the states in question being met. I urge that the government of Canada and the government of British Columbia look upon these water resources as resources that should be developed for the Canadian people first, and then let others have our surplus. We can treat these people with complete equity and fairness and protect our own interests at the same time.
On a number of occasions I have asked the minister questions in respect of article 13 of the Columbia river treaty. I have asked whether the consumptive requirements of the prairie provinces were protected under this article. On those occasions the minister has risen and given what I think it is fair to call very evasive answers. The minister must realize that the diversion of water from the Columbia into the prairie rivers must be accomplished by pumping; then there must be the production of electrical energy to recover the power lost in pumping, and then this water will flow through a number of plants on the rivers in Alberta and Saskatchewan. The minister replied in effect that the rights of the prairie provinces were protected in so far as consumptive requirements were concerned.

No, so far as
consumptive uses are concerned, which is quite different.

The minister never gave me a direct answer in respect of the multiple use requirements, which is a different question. I should like to ask the minister three questions. They are as follows: in the event that 10 or 20 years from now it was decided to divert water from the Columbia into the Saskatchewan for consumptive and non-consumptive uses, and that this water was to flow through a series of hydro plants between the Rockies and its point of use in Saskatchewan or Manitoba and the surplus was to flow on to Hudson bay, is there anything in the Columbia treaty in its present form that could prevent it?
Supply-External Affairs Has the government of Canada ascertained the views of the United States government on this matter, and are they the same as the views of the Canadian government?
If not, will the Canadian government ascertain the views of the United States government on this matter before the treaty is signed? I ask these questions because they are being asked by people in Saskatchewan and organizations that represent the persons interested in the consumptive use of water on the prairie provinces.
In conclusion I have one more question. In view of the written promise of the Prime Minister of Canada that a Liberal government would not make a decision with regard to the Columbia river treaty prior to the persons directly concerned being consulted, can the minister assure the house that this promise will be kept and no decision will be made until those persons interested have been consulted and their views heard?

Mr. Chairman, after listening carefully to the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), who dealt with the question of diplomatic relations, I should like to say a few words on the occasion of the consideration of the estimates of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin).
Since efforts have been made in these last few years, through the ecumenical council, to bring closer relations between representatives of the various religious denominations throughout the world, it seems advisable to mention here a request which was made on several occasions by Canadian organizations, in the province of Quebec as well as in the other provinces, to the effect that an ambassador should be appointed to facilitate relations with the Vatican and to interpret the various religious viewpoints in Canada.
In my opinion, it would be more than ever advisable, especially since it is endeavoured by all possible means to bring together the different religious faiths in the world in order to help solve the religious, political and economic problems throughout the world.
I should like to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs this question. Does the Canadian government intend to take this opportunity to appoint in the near future an ambassador to the Vatican?

Mr. Chairman I promised the other day, after returning from the NATO meeting, in answer to a question by the Leader of the Opposition, that on my estimates I would make a report on that meeting. The hon. member for Oxford has

Supply-External Affairs renewed the request of the Leader of the Opposition, which I am very happy to fulfil at this time.
The ministerial meetings of NATO, are in camera. It is not possible to give a detailed account of the matters discussed or of the decisions reached. However, to the extent that it is possible to give an indication of our discussions, I may say that this particular meeting took place at the end of a rather unusual year in international affairs.
At the beginning of that year we had what the Soviet union foreign minister has called the Caribbean affair or the situation in Cuba, and the actions taken by the United States with regard to the installation on the island of Cuba of Soviet offensive nuclear weapons in October, 1962. Since that time other matters of interest have taken place. We have the partial nuclear test ban treaty which was agreed by the foreign ministers of the United States, the Soviet union and the United Kingdom in August. This partial test ban treaty has since been supported by 107 nations or more. Then there was the agreement between the United States and the Soviet union with regard to the banning of weapons of mass destruction in outer space.
These are matters of great significance in relation to the general problems that face us at the present time. Perhaps in themselves they do not represent the full achievement which is desirable, but certainly as demonstrations of the detente that exists they must not be discounted.
Advantage was taken at this meeting and against this background, to discuss the general state of east-west relations. It was well that this should be done, because at this meeting there were a number of new representatives of governments. Since the previous ministerial meeting there had come into office some new heads of government, including a new prime minister in the United Kingdom, a new chancellor in West Germany, a new president in the United States and a new prime minister in Italy. In addition to these heads of government there were at the NATO table a number of new foreign ministers, including of course the foreign secretary of the United Kingdom, Mr. Butler.
I took advantage of the meeting in Paris the other day to invite Mr. Butler, at some time convenient to him, to visit Canada. I hope this visit will take place in the relatively near future. I took advantage also of the presence of Mr. Saragat, a distinguished Italian statesman who has taken an active part in the politics of his country over a long period and who is now its foreign minister and vice premier, to ask him to come to Canada at his convenience.
[Mr. Martin (Essex East).)
We agreed at the ministerial meeting to take advantage of every opportunity to extend the area of agreement with the Soviet union. We were not all agreed as to the nature of the period of tranquillity which exists and as to whether it is in fact a detente. I am impressed by the suggestion that there is a difference between a detente and a state of actual peace; and bearing in mind that refinement it must be obvious that there is today a detente between east and west. We must take advantage of this to further reduce the risks of conflict between the Soviet union and the western nations.

When the minister refers to a detente between the Soviet countries and the western countries does he mean that in the strictly military sense or in the political sense, in the broader meaning of the word, and also in the economic sense?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I meant in the general relations which prevail between east and the west. Between the Soviet union on the one hand and the western world on the other, there is a disposition, we believe, to try to eliminate possibilities of conflict, particularly in this era of nuclear independence.
The minister means military conflict?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I hope my hon. friend will permit me to examine the nature of this situation as I see it. We are convinced that, for a number of reasons, the Soviet union is desirous of improving its relations with the western world, we in turn are anxious to make sure that there is proper reciprocity.
There are a number of reasons for the exisence of this detente. It is not necessary to traverse what I said when my estimates were introduced. We believe there are a number of contributing factors in this developing situation. I took occasion then to express the view that commercial, cultural and scientific contacts could be important in bringing about a further harmonization between east and west.
While the situation of detente exists, it is true that at the same time the major political problems that divide east and west remain unresolved. There is still a divided Germany. There is still a divided Berlin. There are the problems centered in Indo China, particularly in Viet Nam and in Laos, and the situation developing in Cambodia. There continue to be problems in the Middle East, and there are, of course, problems in the commonwealth country of Malaysia and the attitude toward that country adopted by Indonesia, notably by the president of Indonesia. So while on the one hand there

is this detente, the problems that divide east and west have yet to be resolved. There is therefore no justification for overstatement; nor is there any justification for failure to appreciate the extent to which progress is being made in relations between east and west.
The 18 nation disarmament committee, will be holding its session in Geneva on January 20. We at the North Atlantic Treaty Organization meeting gave consideration to some aspects of the problems that will arise at Geneva. There is a strong disposition to take advantage of the Geneva meeting to see if further agreement, even on a limited scale, might not be achieved on disarmament. I think it is wise to be realistic and to recognize the realities that may not make possible a wide area of agreement on disarmament at this time. I indicated that Canada would pursue its objectives, in concert with its NATO allies, trying to reach as wide a measure of agreement as possible on disarmament, taking advantage of the agreement that was reached in Moscow on the partial nuclear test ban treaty.
We will stress at the Geneva meeting, as I indicated at the Paris meeting, the importance we attach to the proposal for the establishment of control posts on each side of the iron curtain as a means of reducing the risks of surprise attack. This matter was given attention by ministers attending the NATO meeting, and between now and the disarmament meeting to be held in January, there will be further consideration of some practical aspects of the proposal for the establishment of control posts and inspection teams on both sides of the iron curtain.
I wish to say that there is no justification for the view, so widely stated in the newspapers, about the state of disunity in NATO. Each member of the organization took occasion at this last meeting to affirm his country's belief and confidence in the integrity and the purposes of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. There were no exceptions to this reaffirmation of confidence in the purposes of the alliance.
There are differences, of course, as to method, but this is inevitable in any alliance that is predicated upon the membership of nation states that are free. But there can be no doubt that NATO represents a group of nations dedicated to the fundamental basis of the organization, which they recognize as an essential instrument for the preservation of peace, and for their defence in the light of the situation that prevails in the world at the present time.
I think I properly characterize this meeting by saying that the relative tranquillity that has existed in the world for the last 12
Supply-External Affairs months, gave the foreign ministers in attendance an opportunity to carefully evaluate their relations with the east, with the Soviet union. This involved a consideration of commercial policies. It involved a consideration of the use and the terms of credit that should be extended to communist countries in trade in non-strategic goods. It also involved an appreciation of the results of some of the activities of the United Nations that are of concern to NATO.
I should like to tell the committee that there should not be any reserve in the minds of hon. members about this country's support for NATO or about the wide measure of support for the alliance by all the member states which constitute that organization.

Mr. Chairman, I will not take much of the committee's time. I am sure all hon. members of the committee were interested in hearing the resume given by the Secretary of State for External Affairs regarding the recent NATO meeting. I wanted to ask the minister just three brief questions. The first is with reference to the role of NATO in economic matters. The press reports certainly gave the impression that this was a lacklustre meeting of the NATO ministers, largely because, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs himself has said, we have reached a detente and the primary purpose on which NATO was predicated, is much less serious now than it has been for many years. This is the criticism that many of us raised at the time NATO was formed, that an organization that is built upon a negative, namely fear of military aggression and nothing else, is likely to lose its centripetal force when the threat of aggression diminishes.
This is why many of us argued so strongly at the time that article 2 of the treaty ought to be the important and the long range objective of NATO. I would predict that unless NATO is able to assume a more positive role, as the danger of military aggression relaxes NATO is very likely to disintegrate. I want to ask the minister whether the economic role which was envisaged for NATO is now going to be left entirely to O.E.C.D., or whether there were any discussions with a view to giving NATO some effective and positive economic role in world affairs.
The other question I want to ask the minister is with reference to the attitude of the NATO countries concerning the shipment of arms and military equipment to South Africa and to Portugal. I would like to have it clear as to Canada's position in this regard. What steps are we taking to make absolutely sure that no Canadian arms or military supplies are going to either South Africa or Portugal? Also, what member nations of NATO are

Supply-External Affairs taking definite steps to see that armaments are not going to Portugal and South Africa? Would the minister tell us which nations have refused to place such an embargo on this type of shipments? I would appreciate it if we could get some information from the minister on those points, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, I have been asked a number of questions. First of all I should like to deal with the questions asked by the hon. member for Kootenay West with regard to the Columbia. In this connection I note the question put to me today on the orders of the day by the hon. member for Kootenay East as to the progress of the discussions on the Columbia river project, the meeting yesterday with the United States negotiators.
I believe that the discussions held yesterday advanced this project more than at any time since we began this series of negotiations. As a result of the progress made and the agreement reached, we are now in a position to put into documentary form material for consideration by our respective governments. This will be followed by a meeting to be held in Washington about January 9. I should like to say, Mr. Chairman, that at yesterday's meeting those of us who represented the Canadian position, the government of Canada and the province which is owner of the resource, maintained a joint position in our negotiations with the United States.
The Columbia river project is a very important one. It is one of the major projects that has been considered by any Canadian government. It is a matter of great importance not only to British Columbia but to Canada as a whole. It is a matter of great importance in the relations between the United States and Canada. I may assure the committee that in the negotiations the interests of this country are, of course, carefully observed.
My hon. friend asked me three questions. The three questions that he put to me today were contained in a letter dated December 16 which I received from the premier of Saskatchewan. I shall be replying to that letter in the course of the next few days.
On the first question, as to the situation 10 or 20 years from now with regard to the right of use of the waters of the Columbia for what my hon. friend called consumptive purposes, I can say-this is obviously a hypothetical question-that it will depend upon the situation at that time. But in the context of the question in the language used by the premier of Saskatchewan, the decision would have to rest in this instance with the

government of British Columbia. This is obviously a matter on which only the owner of the resource could make a decision.
As to the question of diversion from the Columbia for purposes of irrigation, there is no doubt about the position under the treaty. My hon. friend said that when he asked this question some time ago, I was evasive. I do not think I was evasive in regard to this question. I was not able to give my hon. friend answers to all his questions, because most of them obviously had to do with matters that were then under negotiation. But on the question of interpretation of the treaty there has been no evasion. Article 13 (1) is clear. No loss of right to divert waters for irrigation purposes is contained in the treaty, because the expression "consumptive use" provides for irrigation. This right would be open to Canada in the future, if it were thought that this resource, the Columbia, was desired for irrigation purposes by any particular province in western Canada.
In confirmation of what I have just said there is the testimony of General John Itsch-ner of the United States army corps of engineers before a committee of congress; it said in substance what I have just indicated, namely that neither country will be denied the right of diversion from the Columbia of water for irrigation purposes, which under the treaty are defined as consumptive use.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam asked me about the economic aspects of NATO. Article 2 of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization provides for collaboration among the members of NATO along lines which would promote their mutual economic interests. As he knows, Canada was among those nations which have taken a strong position in urging action toward the implementation of article 2. However, the situation within recent years and more particularly since the establishment of the organization for economic co-operation and development, has considerably advanced.
It is not correct to say that within NATO itself there has been complete implementation of article 2, but some of the ancillary and auxiliary actions taken by members of NATO in the organization for economic co-operation and development go a long way to cover what has not been done under article 2. O.E.C.D. is an organization made up not only of members of NATO. It is made up not only of members of the European economic community and E.F.T.A., but includes two European nations which are not in either of these European eonomic groupings and, in addition, Japan, the United States and Canada. I attended the O.E.C.D. meeting, as my hon. friend knows, about a month ago, and from what I saw at that meeting and from

what I have been able to learn since taking on this particular ministerial responsibility I think that O.E.C.D. will very largely meet our demands tor the kind of co-operation among NATO member states which has not been fully satisfied under article 2 of NATO.
In addition to O.E.C.D. there is the Kennedy round, the proposal for a 50 per cent linear tariff cut, an initiative which we have welcomed and which we regard as very important for international economic relations, both for the developing countries and for the developed nations.
In addition to this there are the GATT discussions, and the United Nations trade and development conference, which will be held in the spring and will be presided over by a very distinguished Latin American Dr. Pre-hisch, the former governor of the bank in the Argentine. This conference will not only provide the opportunity to consider the economic interests of countries in the O.E.C.D., but as well the relations between members of that group and the developing nations of the world. This will have a very important bearing on the whole question of external aid; because while we all support the principle of external aid on a bilateral basis, I think most of us recognize that to do something fundamental to help the developing countries will require some effort to touch their productive systems and to touch their whole economies. There is no avenue by which this can more effectively be accomplished than by the future trading patterns which are established between these countries and the developed countries of the world.
In answer to the second question of the hon. member for Bumaby-Coquitlam, may I say that Canada has acted on the decision of the security council with regard to the embargo on arms. The Canadian government, in answer to the note of the secretary general on August 19 pursuant to a decision of the United Nations security council, replied on October 21 in these words:
It has for several years been the policy of the Canadian government not to permit the shipment of arms to South Africa which might be used for the enforcement of a policy of apartheid. Following the security council resolution the Canadian government has decided that it will not authorize the acceptance of any new orders from South Africa for items of military equipment, or permit the shipment of such equipment to South Africa.
A similar statement was made with regard to Portugal, the exception in the case of Portugal being confined to arms for use by Portugal in her capacity as a member of NATO. With regard to the use of arms to further her colonial policies there is a prohibition. The Canadian government informed the secretary general on October 18 that no
Supply-External Affairs military assistance has been given by Canada to Portugal since November, 1960; and with regard to sales on a commercial basis, it had been the policy of the Canadian government since 1960 not to permit the export to Portugal or to the territories under Portuguese administration of any arms or equipment which in the opinion of the Canadian authorities would be used for military purposes in Portuguese overseas territories. The Canadian government intends to continue this policy. I made a similar statement along these lines in this house on October 21.

Before the minister leaves that point may I ask him this question. How is it possible to make sure that arms shipped to Portugal under NATO commitments are not transferred and used for colonial repression?

It is a matter for each nation on its own responsibility. We have declared what we are doing. We can only assume that formal declarations of policy by other countries are being observed by those countries. It is the responsibility, I suppose, of the collective organizations concerned to see whether or not there is compliance by the various countries which have made replies to the requests of the secretary general.
I do not know whether the minister has my point.
With regard to the number of countries, I cannot tell my friend which countries of NATO have placed an embargo on arms for South Africa; I have not that information before me at the moment.

I do not think the minister has the point I was putting to him a moment ago. I understood him to say that Canada had placed an embargo on the delivery of arms to Portugal or to any of her overseas territories which might be used for repressive measures, but that we still permit the shipment of arms to Portugal if they come within the category considered to be necessary for the fulfillment of that country's NATO commitments. I wonder how the government satisfies itself that arms going to Portugal to meet NATO commitments are not used for colonial repressive purposes. What criteria are used?

We rely on our NATO partner, Portugal. They know the nature of the embargo. We have no reason to assert that they have not conformed to the requirements of Canadian government policy. If the situation were otherwise we would not hesitate to discuss the matter with the government of Portugal.

Supply-External Affairs
Can the minister assure the house that obsolete or out of date weapons which are replaced by new weapons from Canada are not taken out of Portugal and used for colonial repression?

I would prefer to answer that question by directing myself to what I should think would be a better form of question, I know of no reason for concluding that Portugal is acting contrary to the policy of the Canadian government in this matter.
I take it that the minister cannot assure the house that obsolete weapons replaced by new weapons supplied by Canada are not being shipped to Portuguese possessions overseas for colonial repression.

The hon. member looks at me with a delightful air of infallibility. I can only assure the committee that I know of no justification for the conclusion that Canadian government policy is not being observed by Portugal. This, surely is an answer which ought to satisfy the hon. member.

The minister has been giving the committee his opinions about international affairs. He has talked about states of peace and detentes. I ask him again, referring to his use of the word "detente", whether he means to say that the Soviet union has placed an embargo on economic, ideological and revolutionary penetration in Latin America and other parts of the world.

I thank the hon. member for repeating his question. It is true I did not fully understand its implications when it was first put. When I introduced my estimates I dealt with this matter. I said then that while I believe there is an improvement in east-west relations, this does not mean that the Soviet union has abandoned its ideological objectives either at home or abroad. There is serious difference between the Soviet union and the Chinese people's republic. However, this in turn should not lead Canada or any other western country to an unwarranted position as a result of the differences between these two giants of the communist world.

I have one specific matter which I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. As he knows, the United Nations has been placing special emphasis on aid to underdeveloped countries; in fact I believe it was the late President Kennedy who in one of his early speeches to the United Nations assembly referred to the importance of dealing with this matter as quickly as possible. I believe that as a result a special
[Mr. Martin (Essex East).!
designation was given to the programs he espoused, namely the United Nations development decade.
Canada has responded in this area during recent years, particularly under the leadership of the former minister for external affairs, Hon. Howard Green, who was a distinguished member of this house for so many years, and there have been some improvements in this regard. I do not wish to take up the time of the committee enumerating the schemes which were launched during the time of Hon. Howard Green. However, I cannot refrain from doing so. In 1960 the external aid office was established, and about the same time the basic aid to Colombo plan countries was increased from $34 million to $50 million. Unfortunately there was a temporary cutback in this figure following the exchange prices of a year ago. I am pleased to see that the amount of money involved in this cut has now been restored.
Then there was participation in the special fund of 1959, and there was also the program of aid to the West Indies started in 1958, which over a period of some five years has resulted in a contribution of some $10 million to those countries. Then there was the commonwealth scholarship and fellowship plan which was commenced in 1960, which amounts to $1 million a year and results in an average of 200 scholarships being made available each year. Then there was the other program which was launched in 1961, designed to assist the newly independent French speaking countries of Africa. It was an education assistance program and involved an annual expenditure of about $300,000 a year directed to 15 newly independent countries of Africa. Then in 1960, in the wake of the challenge presented by the late President Kennedy, Canada agreed to offer assistance known as the special commonwealth aid program to countries like Tanganyika, Ghana, the Congo, and so on. This amounted to a contribution of $10.5 million over a three year period. Then there was the launching of the export finance program in January, 1961, which I believe represented a step forward in this field. So, generally speaking, Canada has endeavoured to carry its load in this area of assistance.
There is, however, one item that I should like to bring to the minister's attention at this time, and it concerns the emergency assistance program which was made available to Hong Kong in 1962 and which amounted to about $485,000, consisting largely of a contribution of skim milk and canned meat products which were in surplus in Canada at that time. The minister knows that I have been pursuing this subject in the house since July 24 of this year. I have asked a series of questions and

the minister has constantly delayed giving specific replies. In the early stages of my questioning he seemed to suggest that he agreed there was a continuing state of emergency. We know the importance of Hong Kong as a bastion of the free world. The most recent statement the hon. gentleman made in this regard was to the effect that he would give me a complete and definitive report during the consideration of his estimates. I wonder if he is prepared now to do that.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend is *quite correct. The fact is that there is no program of assistance to this area at the present time.

My question is, will consideration be given to such a program? I am sure the minister is aware that Hong Kong suffered a disastrous drought last year which *compounded the problems in that part of the world. It was my privilege to visit Hong Kong last May; and even though this country, being on the fringe of the Orient, is somewhat better off than other countries, it was quite obvious that there was a desperate need for assistance of this kind.
I was impressed too by the high regard in which Canada is held there, largely because of this important emergency food program and also because of the visit of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle to that country some two years ago, when he established very important personal relationships with the people there on the occasion of the first sale of wheat to communist China. I am sure that the friendly and cordial relations which were largely established by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle during his visit have made it possible to continue this important wheat market for western Canadian farmers.
I am sure the minister is aware that there is a real emergency there, and in this decade when we are reaching out in every possible and conceivable way to deal with these problems of extreme urgency I am sure he will agree that the problems of the have-not countries, representing 80 per cent of the world, where people are ill clothed and ill fed, is one with regard to which Canada should assist in every way possible. With our surplus skim milk and our surplus canned goods products, it seems to me this is an area where Canada could quite easily provide continuing assistance.

Mr. Chairman, I have one question for the minister, and if I put it now it may facilitate the individual votes in his department going through very quickly. Some years ago, primarily as a result of the activities of the Canadian NATO parliamentary group, I believe, an action committee was
Supply-External Affairs formed under the chairmanship of Mr. Van-Zeeland of Belgium to establish an Atlantic institute. That committee operated and eventually did establish the Atlantic institute which I believe now has offices in Paris. One of the distinguished members of the original action committee was the present Prime Minister of Canada. I am wondering what the attitude of the Canadian government is now toward the institute. Do they recognize it? There is no evidence in the estimates of any government support for the institute. What is the attitude toward this body now?

Mr. Chairman, the government continues to have an interest in the Atlantic co-ordinating committee and makes a grant toward its operations. The grant is in the amount of $2,500. I have had suggestions recently from interested parties in this organization for an increase in the grant, particularly in view of the fact that the institute will be holding meetings in Canada some time in the month of September, 1964, I believe. Consideration is being given to this request.
We recognize that the Atlantic institute, itself and the co-ordinating committee, perform a useful assignment in educating and informing the public about NATO, in research into the various purposes and activities of NATO, and generally in promoting the solidarity of the people of the north Atlantic area. I assure my hon. friend that this matter is one which engages our interest and will continue to do so.
While I am on my feet perhaps I might supplement my answer to the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam. We have not given any military assistance to Portugal since 1960. Assurances were requested from Portugal that it would not send Canadian NATO mutual aid arms or equipment to its overseas territories. From conversations I had in Paris the other day with the Portuguese foreign minister I have every reason to think that this is in fact being observed.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have three questions. They are not related to each other, but it will save time if I put them all to the minister now and he can answer all three at once when he gets to his feet. First, what comment has he to make on the reports that the French embassy in Ottawa interfered in some way with the decision that Trans-Canada Air Lines recently had to make? Second, what comment has he to make on the letter which he wrote to the Canadian Jewish Congress in reply to the appeal made to him by that body? I am referring, of course, to the exchange of letters to which I referred before we broke for lunch. My third question relates to something in the future. It has

Supply-External Affairs been indicated to us that the Prime Minister will be making a visit to Washington some time in January. Can the Secretary of State for External Affairs tell us if this has been made firm, and whether the agenda of that metting is something that can be given to us at this time?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, with regard to the French embassy, I made a statement in the house the day before yesterday. I intimated that when I was in Paris on Monday and Tuesday of this week I called the Sud-Aviation Company of France and had what I would call satisfactory telephone conversation with regard to a situation which has reached proportions which should not affect good relations between France and Canada. I do not feel I can usefully add to what I said in the house the other day. I think my hon. friend will understand why I believe the question should be left at this point.
With regard to the matter of the Jewish congress letter, I share with my hon. friend, as every member of the house does, a dislike for any form of discrimination practised by any country toward minority groups. We have expressed our condemnation of apartheid in South Africa. The Prime Minister and I as Secretary of State for External Affairs, have in the United Nations, in this house and elsewhere expressed our concern about discrimination which is practised in many areas. Indeed, when I spoke on the question of apartheid in the United Nations I pointed out that it was against Canada's policy to expel any member from the United Nations because of such policies. One of the reasons I gave was that if we were to adopt this practice, we would have to direct our criticisms and take similar action against certain other member states in the United Nations.
The fact that anti-Semitism exists in the Soviet union today is condemned by us with as much vigour as by the hon. member, and I am sure he will agree. This question was dealt with not only in the correspondence between myself and Mr. Michael Garber, president of the Jewish congress; it was also dealt with on November 20 of this year when the Prime Minister made the following statement, as reported in Hansard at page 4957:
I find it particularly unfortunate that any government should find it necessary to resort to those penalties for economic crimes which were abandoned in many countries of the world at least a century ago. Although the penalties have been levied against persons of various nationalities and faiths within the U.S.S.R., the disproportionate number of Jews given severe sentences may reflect the historical tradition of anti-Semitism which has prevailed among the population, even though there is no evidence to suggest a state program encouraging anti-Semitic tendencies.

Then on page 4958 the Prime Minister is reported as follows:
-there is in the Soviet union a deep-seated suspicion of cosmopolitanism, that is a mistrust of elements in the population and particularly of minority and religious elements which the Soviet authorities fear might have international connections and loyalties which could conflict with their allegiance to the U.S.S.R. Because of this consideration, Mr. Speaker, the present government, as did the previous administration, wishes to avoid any official action which, by emphasizing the Soviet suspicion of the international affiliation of the Jews, might provoke further restrictions against the Jewish community in the U.S.S.R.
I appreciate the attitude my hon. friend took this morning. It is an understandable attitude. I, as foreign minister of Canada, in the light of the information at my disposal, in the light of all the circumstances, believe that the exercise of judgment in this matter which we have made is in the interests of the three million Jews in the Soviet union. However, I have noted what my hon. friend said today. The matter will be reviewed again. I may assure him that the course we have taken in this matter was not taken lightly, but was taken in the interests of the Jews in the Soviet union. Nothing would be gained by resorting to spectacular acts of condemnation or criticism which might have consequences perhaps affecting the welfare of the Jewish people who live within the precincts of the Soviet union.
My hon. friend asked me finally about the visit of the Prime Minister to Washington. It is now settled that the Prime Minister will visit President Johnson on January 22, following his visit to General de Gaulle on January 15, 16 and 17. When the Prime Minister was in Washington attending the funeral of the late President Kennedy he had a talk with the President of the United States. As I mentioned the other day in the house, our Prime Minister was the second head of government to be asked to meet with the new president on that memorable day following the tragic death of President Kennedy. I was present at the conversation, so I can attest to the importance which the new President attaches to the relationship of his country to Canada. It was clearly evident to me that the new President is anxious to establish with the present Prime Minister of Canada the closest relations such as those that existed between the Prime Minister and the late President Kennedy.
When the Prime Minister returned from Washington he wrote a personal note to the President of the United States, thanking him for the generous time given by the President on that busy day, almost the first day on which he assumed the great responsibilities that are now his. Since this note was written in the Prime Minister's own hand I do not

have a copy. It was a friendly note, thanking the President for the opportunity to meet him so early and extending to him on behalf of the government and the people of Canada assurances of friendly co-operation in meeting his heavy responsibilities.
I should think it would be desirable, and with the approval of the White House, I now place on the record the reply of the President of the United States. It is dated December 13, 1963 and reads as follows:
Dear Mr. Prime Minister:
I have been heartened by your letter of December 3. It has been a very great encouragement in these last hard weeks to have the sympathy and support of such a neighbour and leader as yourself. Even at the end of that longest of days, it was a help to have a chance to talk with you, and I now look forward with pleasure to the prospect of our meeting in the new year.
Relations between our two countries are so intimate, numerous and varied that for each of us the relationship is really unique. I fully agree with what you were the first to say-that the intimacy of our connection in no sense permits us to take our relations for granted. I have been close to a number of the specific questions which have been pursued with new understanding and energy on both sides since the meeting at Hyannis Port, and I can assure you again of my determination to keep our relations moving in the spirit which President Kennedy and you established then.
Both in this purpose and in wider problems of our common concern for peace, it is already a help to me to know that you and I can talk to each other frankly and work easily together. It is true that the burdens of this office are heavy, and its responsibilities not limited to the boundaries of this nation-and that makes it all the more important that the man who works here should have the help of friends like yourself.
This brings my warm thanks and the very best wishes of Mrs. Johnson and myself to Mrs. Pearson and you for Christmas and the new year.
I am sure, Mr. Chairman, that the committee will recognize the importance of the visit of the Prime Minister not only to France but to the United States on January 22. I had a discussion last Sunday with Mr. Rusk about this visit. It will be a working visit. The subjects under discussion will cover a wide area. It is of course not possible at this stage to talk about those. I thank my hon. friend for asking this question and giving me an opportunity to make this statement.

Mr. Chairman, as the minister seems ready to answer in great detail the questions which are being asked, I am going to remind him briefly of the one I asked a little while ago. Does the minister intend to appoint soon an ambassador to the Vatican?

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member knows very well that when an announcement has to be made by the government, the occasion and the time for that announcement are its own choice.
Supply-External Affairs
Could the minister tell us if any effort is being made at the United Nations to resolve the problems faced by Palestinian refugees in the Near East?

My hon. friend has referred to efforts at the United Nations, and I assume he also means efforts elsewhere, on the part of Canada to try and help resolve the differences between certain countries in the Middle East. With regard to the United Nations, may I, first, say that I am very grateful to my parliamentary secretary, to the members of the Canadian delegation and to the observers from the House of Commons who attended the last general assembly, for the distinguished and valuable services they rendered to Canada at the general assembly.
We continue to harbour a sincere interest in trying to bring together the representatives of the United Arab Republic and Israel. This has been the object of Canadian policy for a long time. I can only say to my hon. friend that our efforts in this connection are continuing.
Could the minister tell us whether any progress is being made toward a permanent solution of this problem?
I do not think I can add to what I have said.

In his earlier remarks the minister made reference in summary form to a few of the situations in southeast Asia. I did not hear him make any reference to Malaysia and the situation which has arisen between that country and Indonesia, with the so-called confrontation by President Sukarno. What assurances of assistance or help has Canada given to Malaysia as a fellow member of the commonwealth?

I am sure the committee generally would agree with me when I express the hope that there will be no deterioration in the situation which confronts the new Federation of Malaysia. It would be tragic if any initiative taken by any country in southeast Asia were to interfere with the development of the new federation. Malaysia, of course, is a member of the commonwealth. At the United Nations, commonwealth members had occasion to discuss Malaysia's problems and its present concerns vis-a-vis some of its neighbours. This matter is one that engages the interests of the commonwealth as a whole, particularly those of the United Kingdom, Australia and New Zealand; the problem is being carefully watched by members of the commonwealth, including Canada.
Item agreed to.

Supply-Legislation
44a. Contribution to the Atlantic institute, $4,000.

I would like to ask the minister whether this vote is in addition to the $2,500 grant he referred to in reply to my earlier question. This is a vote for $4,000 for the Atlantic institute. Is this an additional grant?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Consideration is being given to an addition. The money was provided in the supplementary estimates of 1963-64 in the amount that my hon. friend mentions, and consideration is being given to a request for further assistance, but no decision has been taken.

Item agreed to.
SO. Salaries and expenses, $652,600.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: The minister was not able to be present in the committee on external affairs when we put the report together, but I am sure he has read it and found it a useful and interesting document. I would like to draw his attention to the fact that two main recommendations made by the committee related to external aid, and that increased money be found to recruit personnel for this important work. I would like to enlist the minister's support for these recommendations.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In connection with the external aid office, I would like to congratulate the minister for his interest in and support of the Canadian university service overseas, and to enjoin upon him that he continue his earnest efforts to soften the hearts of treasury board and get a grant for this very worth-while organization.
Item agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

Mr. Chairman, I had intended to go into this quite extensively, but I do not think the house is disposed that way so I will forgo my intention. However, we have done this a number of times. Legislation is always the last item, and I would like to say a few words on it because it is a very important field and we have not considered it extensively for some time. As I said the other night, when the Secretary of State felt I was only holding this up for one of my

colleagues, that is not true. There is a decision to be reached in the matter of legislation. The Speaker of the house has this matter under consideration, and the report would indicate that there is an investigation contemplated that would allow the civil service commission to investigate it. The committee had this to say:
Mr. Speaker has requested the organization division of the civil service commission to undertake a complete survey of the Speaker's establishment. This survey, which has been approved by the commissioners of internal economy, is now in progress-
It is rather a study of the structural organization of the House of Commons staff to be followed by an examination of the work methods and procedures.
As I pointed out, we are running an establishment here equivalent to that run by a municipal government with a population of
5,000	to 10,000 people in the municipality. With the 1,000 or more employees we have in the house in various departments, it is an obvious fact that the Speaker and the internal economy commission cannot be expected to act as employer, supervisor and look after the other business that the Speaker obviously has to look after. It seems to me that we are operating under a very archaic system where we have the government itself, in the form of the internal economy commission-
Infernal economy commission.

You can call it infernal, if you wish, because I am quite sure that some of the members of that commission have so much to do that they certainly have not much time to participate in this particular field. One of the problems that arises is the fact that many members of parliament have not really considered the establishment of the House of Commons and parliament hill at all. I have a summary of some of the legislation that affects the parliament buildings. I should like to table it, because I do not wish to take up the time of the committee by reading it. It was prepared by the law branch and refers to the title of the establishment of the House of Commons. I would like to table this document, Mr. Chairman, for insertion in Hansard, if there is no objection.
Agreed.
By whom was this prepared, and under whose authority?
I said it was prepared by the law branch of the House of Commons. It may have been a former Speaker's authority. Well, I could read it, Mr. Chairman.
No.
He isn't the Speaker any more.
Is there any objection to that course being followed, Mr. Chairman?
No.
It is a history of how the property, particularly of how the House of Commons itself, has developed.

Hon. members will have an opportunity to see this and assess what the intention of parliament with regard to the establishment may be in the future. This affects, of course, some of the things I shall mention. I would be willing, if it were thought desirable, to table it as part of my remarks concerning parking facilities and other facilities in connection with the house. This document also deals with the R.C.M.P. services on the hill and some of the duties of the protective staff. The protective staff of the house has grown rapidly since its inception. It is a highly trained and, I think, a very satisfactory staff. It is now handling an immense number of tourists each year as well as the other duties that are allocated to that branch. They have now had added to their number a staff which is servicing the west block, and I suggest they should also have added a staff to handle the east block of the parliament buildings. This staff should be given a higher status than it now has. These officers are not allowed to make arrests. They are not given any authority and do not, of course, have to assume certain responsibilities that a normal police force is asked to assume. These officers should have a status equal to that of our federal police force, because they
Supply-Legislation
are a federal protective staff and should therefore have some of the protections that normal police forces enjoy.
I would suggest that a municipality having 72 constables and officers is a fairly large municipality and this requires the force to be given the same protection as a regular police force. There should be a system whereby grievances can be dealt with and which will deal with the relationships between the force and the body it serves. There have recently been difficulties in the force. These come to the attention of members of parliament, and it seems to me this is not a satisfactory manner in which to handle this problem. I will not go into the details of some of the things that have happened; but it seems to me this is not a good way of operating this force. I am only using it as one of the examples, because there are 15 or 20 departments of a similar nature. I suggest that it may be necessary to bring them under the civil service, as is the case with the other branches, or it may be necessary to organize them into a union and allow them to operate within a union structure.
If it is decided that this problem can be settled in this manner, I personally will be quite happy to act as their agent on a temporary basis until they are organized. I would ask one of the unions of this country for the right to act as their agent, and organize them. I would be happy to do that early in the next session. This of course would create certain problems which I think should be discussed before this is done, because I can see some difficulty in my position, dealing with agents of the crown and applying to the federal labour board for certification. However, I think the problems involved are sufficiently great that if we cannot arrive at a more satisfactory solution I will attempt to do this early in the next session.
There are many other problems. One problem affects the Secretary of State and I think he has perhaps not paid too much attention to it. I refer to that hard working group of people in the house today, the 10 or 11 members of the translation bureau. This bureau comes under the jurisdiction of the Secretary of State. As I understand it, it is part of a larger bureau of translation, but most of them are employed here. I think it is true-and the Secretary of State certainly agrees with this, because he has said many times that it is very difficult to increase this particular staff-that they number-

I see that in this morning's edition of Le Devoir the Quebec civil service is asking for translators and offering salaries starting at $8,400. I should like to know whether this is the same initial salary for translators employed by the House of Commons.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I will answer that question when the estimates for the civil service commission come up a little later in the afternoon.

We thank the Secretary of State for this information. I hope this goes through because I am suggesting that the translators connected with the House of Commons be transferred to the Speaker's department on the hill. I suggest that this is a very good reason for doing this. These translators are highly skilled and have a very difficult job to do. They operate in an international sphere and can transfer from here to many international agencies, including the United Nations. There are approved methods of operation and rates of pay. It is interesting to note that their approved rate of pay in international work is $75 a day-$50 if they work for government. They are supposed to translate for 15 minutes and have a break period; and the hours they translate per day are regulated for. The rates here, until the Secretary of State made his statement, ranged between $7,500 and $8,000 a year.
The problem is this. These ten or eleven people-I will leave out of my consideration the other matters referred to of which I understand Mr. Speaker is well aware-are handling the business of this house. I think it is about this number who handle the translation both in the House of Commons and the Senate. I understand that three out of the ten are usually employed in the Senate. In addition to this there are 12 House of Commons committees and 30 outside commitments. When an agency asks for the services of these translators, even though the House of Commons may be in session they are supplied. I would point out that for the federal-provincial conference on September 9 and 10 five of them were employed on duties outside the House of Commons. Between August 22 and 29 the internal statistical institute employed all ten

of them. If you check the figures, Mr. Chairman, you will find that this has been a problem which has recently resulted in a translator having to go into a committee and translate for four hours, on occasion, without a break. It is bad enough sitting in some of these committees for four hours without having to perform the mental gymnastics of translating from one language to another simultaneously. We have got to the stage where we are not using trained people as technicians. Messengers are operating electrical controls. Caucus rooms are being used for committees without microphones being installed in the right place. The situation is most unsatisfactory. One of these messengers could electrocute himself by using equipment he does not understand. I think we have a responsibility to train them, or to do something with these people before some serious accident occurs through no fault of theirs.
I have used these two examples, but I could go right through the staff. I have been here for some time now and have met many people here. I have talked to quite a number and I think I am safe in saying that I have met some four or five hundred out of the
1,000	employed. I think that whoever does the job which has to be done would have to know all thousand of them, which would be a fuH-time occupation.
I suggest, and I suggest this in all sincerity, that we set up a committee of an interparliamentary nature to assist the internal economy commission. The hon. member for Skeena has a bill to change the structure of the internal economy commission but this has never received much support. I give the government credit on each of the occasions when something has been done. It usually involves money, and therefore there is a government responsibility at stake. But I do not think we should expect to limit that responsibility or to remove it because we are on the legislative side of parliament. I think representatives of the various parties could represent much better the problems existing on parliament hill than is the case today.
There is trouble, Mr. Chairman, in every branch of the House of Commons. We have on standing orders, for instance, a rule which states there should be bilingual law clerks. This has not been the case for some time and this has caused considerable difficulty. The reason that that regulation is on standing orders is because we in this country operate under two completely separate types of legal history, and those trained in the Napoleonic code are not necessarily capable of handling the common law practices enjoyed by many of our provinces. So that we have two distinct types of civil law in this country, as parliament long ago decided on

the matter. We have discussed this question previously, but unfortunately it was in the dying days of the last session, and it was decided that there was insufficient time to settle the matter and it should be discussed in some other way. But the problem is still with us. I suggest it is no one's fault except ours, and I think it is time we did something about it because we have gone beyond our rules in this connection.
There are many other spheres in which we need technical assistance in parliament today. We also need-and I think this is something we ought to look at very shortly-television of our proceedings in the House of Commons. It seems to me rather foolish to have television equipment kept outside in the hall with signs saying "Watch for cables". We spoil the appearance of the parliament buildings with the facilities which are provided. I think it would be wonderful to see television cameras all the time in our public galleries. I should like to see much of the work of parliament televised for the nation. But I think on occasions when parliament does need some coverage we should have proper facilities installed in this building so as to eliminate the temporary facilities provided under the present arrangements.
We have also asked for studios where interviews can be conducted. We also require facilities for radio broadcasting from the House of Commons. We have already mentioned the United Nations and their satisfactory set-up. Those who have attended the United Nations are well aware of it and I imagine are appreciative of it. We also know there should be some research in this regard, and while I am scared of too much research I think the research which would be available to members of parliament in a political sense would assist a member in the performance of his duties and would be of great value. I do not mean that this research should be available to cabinet ministers only. Every time we discuss estimates we see three or four highly trained and certainly highly qualified gentlemen advising the ministers, yet none of this advice is available by way of research to individual members.
Another problem is the translation of letters received from constituents. There is no service provided for this. Unfortunately I am not fluent in either one of the official languages; in one I am at a complete loss. It seems to me that, rather than making arrangements with messengers and other officials in the House of Commons, whom we have to trap in a corner and ask to translate a letter for us, when they are already busy on other duties, there should be a branch capable of doing translation of correspondence for the members.
