The fact is that we come to this house early in the morning and leave it late at night. We are living here, so to speak, and outside this building we have only our sleeping quarters. This causes all types of problems. One of them arose recently in relation to refreshments. I received some credit for the discontinuance of this particular service, but I want to make it clear that I shared this with the Auditor General. I am not alone responsible; I am willing to take only my share of the responsibility. If these matters were discussed, we could arrive at a reasonable arrangement. The arrangement of hiding things for years in odd corners has proved unsatisfactory. I compliment the Sergeant-at-Arms and others who have taken some initiative on their own. I am sorry I may have had some interference in this initiative.
I think the initiative itself was commendable and that the results they are trying to achieve are commendable. However, there has to be support, and a decision reached which is acceptable to everyone in regard to these matters. I believe this could be achieved.
We have been very hard on our Speakers in the last few years. I imagine that in no period of five or six years within the history of parliament have there been more calls on Speakers to make decisions and prepare judgments on particular matters, including subjects which are not normally considered to be part of a Speaker's responsibilities. I believe that for this reason the leader of the house should give us an assurance that a committee will be set up composed of representatives from each of the parties to sit down and discuss some of these problems. I think the time is ripe when this should happen and I may say I intend to write to a number of the international unions involved in regard to these people in the House of Commons. I may be able to secure credentials from many of them and if the problem is not solved in any other way we shall organize the staffs in the House of Commons. It will be a ridiculous situation if a member of parliament stands up and says to the house: Mr. Speaker, you have only until tomorrow night to settle this problem, otherwise there will be a sit-down in these different departments. Maybe this will not happen, but I am personally willing to try it.
I have been interested in this question for some time. In the dying days of parliament we are always making pious statements on this subject but nothing comes of them. I think the only way to bring it to a head is for somebody to do something drastic about it, and I am prepared, if necessary, to be the one who will do something of that nature.

Resign.

If the other business becomes lucrative enough, I may be able to do just that. Without being facetious about this question, it seems to me that the Secretary of State has certainly shown a remarkable capacity for playing chess with the House of Commons. This is a facility which does not come to most people.
We are all pawns.

No, I was not thinking in that sense. I used the expression I did in the sense that the hon. gentleman has been able to make arrangements, to trade and to do the other things necessary to accomplish his purpose. The same procedure could be followed with regard to the matters now before us, and then these problems would cease to exist. I believe that when a problem arises affecting the operations of this house, a problem for which we are, in total, responsible, we should be able to face it and arrive at a solution in a very short space of time.
There is only one other matter I should like to mention and it concerns the training of our staffs. We are seriously in need of assistance. I believe the suggestion made by the Speaker that the head officers at the table be sent to other countries to examine the situation in those countries is an admirable one. It could be a calamity every time we lost an officer of the house, because we have no training, anywhere in the country, which produces men able to fill these positions. This is true with regard to other branches for which a high degree of training is necessary and in preparation for which no satisfactory apprenticeship is possible in another related field. This has been illustrated in the last few weeks by the regrettable illness of one of the officers of the house who sits at the table. I suggest we should complete the complement of our staff and provide a certain amount of stand-by training for others, so that when a vacancy occurs we might be able to fill it with the most competent people available. We must remember that a great deal of the responsibility for the decorum of the house rests with these officers.
If the house would consider these matters and agree to some changes on the lines I have indicated I believe the work of parliament could be carried out more expeditiously and that some of the problems to which I have drawn attention would not occur. If we really think of it, is it not true that the bringing in of staff on a political basis, because a political government was in office, lowers the morale of the department concerned in each case where this happens, because they know that no matter what their competence may be, political considerations, the friends they have, are more important. This is a situation

we do not wish to encourage. It is one we are not going to encourage and I am sure the Speaker will give full consideration to seeing that this problem is solved so that efficiency can remain at a high level.

I should like to bring two matters to the attention of the committee. The first has to do with the report of the standing committee on debates which was filed yesterday morning, pointing out difficulties in connection with the Hansard staff. There are, in essence, two difficulties, one relating to a shortage of reporters and the other to the question of salaries. I would ask that the commissioners of internal economy take action upon these recommendations in the committee's report as quickly as possible.
The second item relates to parking. This is a general question, not a particular one. There is a considerable amount of irritation caused among members of the staff regarding persons who are not connected in any way with parliament but who have parking permits in and around the west block. These people are observed parking their cars and then going to departments downtown somewhere.
I have intended at different times to ask for a return of the individuals who do not have employment on parliament hill but who, nevertheless, have traditional parking permits here. I think this is a situation which can produce a good deal of irritation, particularly at a time when we are short of parking space. It may turn out that there is no one in this category, but I have made inquiries from time to time over the last five or six years and I am convinced there are people in no way connected with parliament who are in possession of parking permits. I should like very much to see this situation resolved, because it causes irritation among staff members, particularly those who live some miles from parliament hill and who have to drive to get here and then seek parking away down behind the Confederation building, though there might be other accommodation available. I should like to see something done about those people who must drive to their work, as opposed to those who do not need to. Those are the two items I should like to mention at this time. The hon. member for Timiskaming has said that there are difficulties in parliament and I am sure there are. But I want to pay a tribute particularly to the protective staff who give courteous consideration throughout the year to the members and to visitors, particularly in the very difficult summer months. I should also like to pay tribute to the excellent work of the supporting services that keep parliament in operation.

Mr. Chairman, I merely want to mention a few facts. For instance, section 4 of Bill No. C-91, which was passed at the end of July or at the beginning of August, reads as follows:
*-there should be allowed to each member of the Senate and House of Commons such actual moving or transportation and travelling expenses between this place of residence or his constituency and Ottawa, and such actual telecommunication expenses incurred while in Ottawa, as each house may by order prescribe for its own members.
Mr. Chairman, as you know, like all hon. members, we constantly have to make phone calls and send telegrams to our ridings, especially on the occasion of winter works, when we must keep in touch with the secretaries and treasurers of municipalities, in order to be informed of any new development.
We note that this legislation was passed at the end of July and that up to now, at the end of December, nothing has been done along the lines I just indicated. We hope that the authorities concerned will be kind enough to take into consideration the fact that members of parliament were requested to pass this act-and it was passed by all- which says, in section 4, that telephone calls and telegrams made or sent to our constituencies, in the ordinary course of a member's business, are to be paid for by the government.
So I ask Mr. Speaker to see that this state of affairs is settled as soon as possible, or at least that we are told why it is not done.
I see that my friends on the Liberal side seem to approve this request, and I am sure all hon. members in this house will ask unanimously that section 4 of Bill No. C-91 which has been passed be put into effect.
We are now considering the Speaker's estimates. I think this is the only opportunity we have in the session to ask him questions. We are happy to do so but, we do not want to take undue advantage of it.
Certain decisions were taken during this session. We accept them and we do not intend to revive the discussions. However, I should like to remind the house of some events which have occurred since these decisions were taken, one of them being the official recognition or non-recognition of the group of 13 members making up the Rallie-ment Creditistes, under the leadership of the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) who sits on this side of the house.
It will be remembered that a decision was reached giving precedence to the group under the leadership of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) over the group of the hon. member for Villeneuve. Now, here

is what transpired since then. The hon. member for Red Deer no longer receives the allowance of $4,000 granted to every political party leader in this house, while the hon. member for Villeneuve is in receipt of it. On the other hand, this order was decided upon ostensibly to comply with seniority. In this connection, I would like to quote a few figures. The 11 members making up the group under the leadership of the hon. member for Red Deer won a total of 23 seats; the group of 13 members under the hon. member for Villeneuve won 27. Moreover, amongst those members, the one who has been at the house for the longest time is the hon. member for Villeneuve, who was elected for the first time in 1946. Moreover, all the members making up the Ralliement Creditistes have been elected at least twice, while two members of the Social Credit party have been elected once only.
I also wish to point out that the leader of the Ralliement Creditistes now receives the $4,000 indemnity, that he has his offices like all party leaders, his secretarial staff, and is entitled to speak on motions like the other leaders of the parties recognized in this house, is entitled to delegations to foreign countries, is a member of the "Head Leaders club", a member of the "Whips club", which means that he is recognized exactly like other party leaders. Besides, we have seniority, as indicated by the figures I quoted a moment ago, the hon. member for Villeneuve having been elected as leader in 1958 while the hon. member for Red Deer was only elected in 1961.
Mr. Chairman, all those arguments give evidence of our seniority and I think that at the next session, the Speaker of the house will have to take his responsibilities and allocate to each group, according to its number and seniority, its rightful place.
I think that at the opening of the next session, the Speaker of the house will have to take his responsibilities and give the Ralliement Creditistes, under the leadership of the hon. member for Villeneuve, the place to which it is entitled.
I respectfully submit this opinion and these arguments which cannot be contradicted because they are facts, and I hope that the Speaker will take them under serious consideration.

Mr. Chairman, I have only one word to say concerning the estimates of the Speaker.
First of all, I wish to congratulate the Speaker for his patience towards me. On occasions, he suggests that the period provided for questions in the house be shortened. From time to time, we do not have the same

opinion. In any event, I wish him to show the same patience during the year 1964.
My remarks will be brief, Mr. Chairman. I want to ask you first whether it would not be possible to provide with simultaneous translation not only the public galleries, but also the second level of the press gallery.
Now, I would ask Mr. Speaker whether it would be possible to give more space to the press gallery. I submit that the members of the press work in difficult conditions, and it seems to me the ideal solution would be to provide them, not only with an individual office, but also with a telephone just like the members of the house, since, like them, they serve the public.
The members of the press gallery organized themselves in an association. I therefore wonder whether it would not be wise, in future, that they have their problems settled by their own association and not by the committee on privileges and elections, or by a member of the house, or by Mr. Speaker himself.
Here is my suggestion. Since journalists are grouped in an association, I think it would be advisable that we, members of the house, should not meddle in their affairs and that they should settle their own problems themselves. Whether a journalist should be admitted or not to the press gallery, I think that journalists are efficient enough to decide that by themselves, according to their own regulations.

Mr. Chairman, I intend to concentrate on one item, the whole question of the Raymond Rodgers case vis-a-vis the press gallery, and my remarks are not for my fellow members so much as for the Speaker.
He will remember that there was a motion of this house to refer the matter to a committee. The committee considered the matter and has presented a report which appears in yesterday's Votes and Proceedings. Pursuant to the order referring to the committee the question of Raymond Rodgers' right to use the facilities of the press gallery, the committee held four meetings and heard the following witnesses: Mr. Raymond Rodgers, Mr. G. J. Connolley, Mr. Arthur Blakely and Mr. Clement Brown. The report states:
The evidence given by Dr. Ollivier before the standing committee on privileges and elections on December 11, 1962, was also tabled before the committee and reproduced as an appendix-
The committee has considered Mr. Rodgers' right to use the facilities of the Canadian parliamentary press gallery and has agreed to recommend:
That while this committee recognizes that parliament has jurisdiction over the public facilities granted the members of the press, we feel that this jurisdiction over the public facilities must 
be exercised through the Speaker or his delegated representative. Therefore, the case of Mr. Rodgers is referred to Mr. Speaker for decision.
The committee further recommends:
That the special committee on procedure and organization, at the next session of parliament, consider the expediency of reviewing the relations now existing between the Speaker and the Canadian parliamentary press gallery on the one hand and the relations now existing between the House of Commons itself and the Canadian parliamentary press gallery on the other hand.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I am speaking with caucus support on this matter. We are very anxious that a decision be made, and we are prepared to support it now or support it at the next session, that will give Raymond Spencer Rodgers, as long as he is the full time correspondent for the St. Catharines Standard, access to the public facilities of the press gallery. There were a number of ironies developed in the evidence and in the voting that went on in the committee. I suppose the most interesting thing was that the voting tended to cross party lines, and I do not believe I am giving away any secrets when I say that this particular recommendation was not unanimous.
I suppose the thing I found most intriguing was the fact that it took us so long to get going because the president of the press gallery, Mr. Connolley, was off to NATO. The whole matter, therefore, was postponed. Then, it turned out, even when Mr. Connolley got back, the press gallery found it necessary to have its main defence presented by a member of the press gallery whom I cannot find either on the executive or the directors of the press gallery. I refer to that great ex-columnist of the Montreal Gazette, Mr. Arthur Blakely. Mr. Blakely carried the defence for the press gallery. The evidence in which I am most interested can be found at page 756 of the report of the proceedings of the committee.
Now, Mr. Chairman, and Mr. Speaker too, I have a particular personal interest in the operations of the press in Canada, and because of that I may say that I was quite intrigued by the Prime Minister's statement today that the government is considering legislation which would prevent the takeover of our press by foreign interests. However, that is an aside. In connection with my interest, I should like to say that I did not want to bring before the committee an individual examination of the basis for belonging to the Canadian parliamentary press gallery and, as a consequence, have the use of the facilities.
I want to put Mr. Blakely's opening statement on the record, to put into context some of the things I want to say about the people who now have the right to use the public

facilities in the press gallery which have been denied to Mr. Rodgers. Mr. Blakely says this:
The term "press gallery" means, in Canada, at least three things. Even in speaking among ourselves, we have to be careful to make it clear which one we have in mind.
The words "press gallery" mean:
1.	The gallery overlooking the House of Commons from which we observe parliamentary proceedings.
I know that many of my colleagues will agree with me when I say that the most outstanding feature about these gentlemen is that when our attendance is criticized during the day or night, we have often found the gallery up there has been bare. The second point is:
2.	The office space, provided to us on the third floor of the centre block, also at public expense, in which we write or otherwise prepare reports on what we have seen and heard in parliament;
I think some members must be aware of the fact that this is one of the worst blocks of housing, it is one of the worst examples of government planning that I have ever seen. It indicates either that the press gallery or the Speakers have been tremendously conservative to allow those conditions to continue, but they are conditions provided at public expense.
The third item Mr. Blakely put forward was:
3.	The Canadian press gallery itself, a professional association which, while not of parliament, has been so close to parliament since confederation that William Lyon Mackenzie King defined it as an "adjunct" of parliament.
Now, those are the three descriptions that Mr. Blakely puts forward. Here, we have a situation where a young man, as the full time correspondent of the St. Catharines Standard, is denied these facilities. This is not his full time work, but so far as the St. Catharines Standard is concerned, he is their full time correspondent. This is a relatively small newspaper in a very prosperous town. They have hired him to do this particular work which consists, usually, of three or four stories a week and sometimes as little as two. However, he does send copy from this place to a legitimate daily newspaper and that copy appears several times a week. I might say that the copy he sends tends to be topical, that is it tends to follow things going on in the house. This is important to the point I want to make.
Now, the press gallery is denying Mr. Rodgers entry on the basis that he does not meet membership qualifications under article II, section (a) of their constitution. This is really the key point. The article reads:

be restricted to persons who earn the major portion of their income through the writing or broadcasting of parliamentary or government news or comment as full-time salaried staff representatives of one or more daily newspapers, radio or television stations or systems, or a recognized news service, sending thereto dispatches regularly; and to persons assigned to work in Ottawa as a resident correspondent of a periodical of national and international standing.
This section, Mr. Speaker, embraces a very wide range. You have broadcasters, telecasters and writers for daily newspapers, weekly newspapers and periodicals both national and international. Every one admits that the St. Catharines Standard is a legitimate Canadian daily newspaper. We have it put on the record that the newspaper wants Rodgers as its representative. Rodgers fails to meet these membership qualifications because he is candid enough to admit that being correspondent for the St. Catharines Standard is not his full time job. It brings him in, he said, somewhere around 40 per cent of his income. One of the contentions Rodgers put to us was that he does not belong to the press gallery association, that is, the part Mr. Blakely had in part 3 of the club. He does not particularly worry about having access to the gallery, but he wants access to a mail slot and to the distribution facilities that are provided through public expense in the press gallery down the way.
I want to go through some of the members of the present press gallery to point out the discrimination that exists in this case through the denial and our failure, or Mr. Speaker's failure, to give this accredited person from a legitimate daily newspaper the right to access. I want to start off the list with Blair Fraser of Maclean's magazine. He is a very well known writer and he writes for a periodical which as I understand it, and I got this information from one of his colleagues, has a two and a half to three weeks deadline. In other words, his need for current copy or, say, for press releases or the blues, is really not very large. Even his need to be in his seat in the press gallery watching the House of Commons, and even though he is often in it, I suggest has nothing very topical about it and there is no great urgency for him to be here, because he has this two week deadline. One other point needs to be mentioned. Mr. Fraser and another man from Maclean's, Mr. Newman, write on very many other subjects relating to public affairs and not necessarily related to the House of Commons.
The next name I want to point out is Walter Scott who writes for the Toronto Star Weekly. This is a large newspaper which comes out once a week and has a circulation of about 800,000. He is down here part of

the time and, incidentally, he wrote an article recently about the Minister of National Health and Welfare. On the average he turns out, relating to parliament and its activities, according to what I can find in an analysis of that paper, no more than one article every month or so. Here again he has been accepted. He is fine, even though most of his duties do not relate to the house, and I am sure he does not earn most of his income as someone covering parliament. But he is fine; he is accredited; he is in. I have nothing against Mr. Scott, who happens to be a friend of mine, but this is an example of the discrimination.
Now I want to go a bit further and pick out a gentleman for whom I have a great admiration and who has been very kind to me. That is Mr. Robert McKeown who writes for Weekend magazine. He is an active member of the press gallery. He is fine. He roams the world doing stories for Weekend magazine, but again I have checked up and on the average he writes less than six stories a year that have any application to the House of Commons or even to work here in Ottawa. A great deal of the kind of work he is doing has nothing whatever to do with Ottawa and the Ottawa scene, but he has membership in the press gallery. Rodgers cannot comply with this magic constitution but Mr. McKeown can. I put it to you that Mr. McKeown's deadline must be at least six or seven weeks. There is no need for him to have this access to blues or press releases. He is not in any kind of a hurry as compared with a man working for a daily newspaper, but it is O.K.; he has got them; it is fine.
I am hoping to put into hon. members' minds the thought that when you examine the range of people working in the press gallery and the kind of work they are doing, there is discrimination here that was not brought out in the committee. That was partly my responsibility because I did not want to get into this question of who does belong to the press gallery.
I want to take a couple of other people, Mr. Warren Baldwin for the Financial Times and Mr. Clive Baxter who works for the Financial Post. Both are well known, capable writers. They write for weeklies and happen to be in competition with each other. Both of them do report the day to day happenings but they tend to be at a little more than arm's length from the average radio or newspaper reports. My point here again is that these men have a deadline that is set for them, and it is not the daily deadline Rodgers may have to meet. Yet they have the advantage. They qualify for membership in the press gallery, and not Rodgers.

Now I want to turn to Time magazine. Time magazine has two members in the press gallery, Jack Beal and Richard Gwyn. I have no quarrel with the fact that they are entitled to the same privileges as many of these other fine gentlemen I have mentioned; but what I point out to you, Mr. Chairman and Mr. Speaker, is that they prepare copy that goes into some kind of masticator, some master digest in Montreal or Toronto, and that in no real sense are they anything more than, you might say, humble people who prepare the basis for what Time finally puts out in its mint condition. There is no urgency about the kind of work they do except in relation to their own weekly deadline.
There is no great need for them to have these facilities, current facilities, that are denied to Rodgers. In fact these gentlemen, and this is understandable, spend a great deal of their time going around Ottawa interviewing people; in other words, getting background, this depth that Time is always searching for. This is fine. This is what their publisher wants them to do. That is part of the Time approach to things. That is great, but their need for having the use of the facilities that are denied to Rodgers is not comparable at all, and I want them to know that.
Mr. Chairman, one of the things when you look at this list is that you realize that the facilities in the gallery-and Mr. Blakely was candid enough to acknowledge this-tend to be hogged by the big newspapers. The Toronto Star and the Toronto Telegram are examples, where they take up much more space, maybe space in relation to their circulations, but that of course should not be the basis on which public facilities are supplied; and I put it to you that the St. Catharines Standard is every bit as important as the Toronto Star and the Toronto Telegram to the member of parliament, to the constituents and to the country as a whole, and yet they cannot qualify.
The Star usually has three to four men circulating around here. They have the use of the gallery but here is this young fellow from the St. Catharines Standard and he cannot even get in to have a little position about four inches by six inches, where he can pick up his mail, press releases and the blues. If you look at this matter in this regard and look through this list-and I challenge the Speaker to do this-and look at some of the people who have membership, and then take a look at the fact that Rodgers is producing copy for a Canadian daily newspaper, there is something terribly discriminatory about the kind of constitution which comes up with this kind of block.

There is one other very touchy element I want to get into, and this relates to the fact to belong to the press gallery is not necessarily, as Roy Thomson found on getting a television licence in Scotland, a licence to print money, but it is a fact that to belong to the press gallery and have the use of its facilities gives you an opportunity to extend your income, and to diversify, as some members of the press gallery have done. Gerald Waring is an outstanding example of this and his colleague, Peter Stursberg is another. There is no criticism of this, but the point is when the use of these public facilities is denied to someone it also means he is blocked off from developing his own income in this particular field. When a press gallery association refuses its membership, and refuses to consider the sharing of the public facilities with someone who is an accredited representative of a daily newspaper, it raises in my mind and in the minds of others the feeling that perhaps they do not want anyone else to get in on their opportunities. I may be exaggerating on this particular point, but it is certainly in the mind of Mr. Rodgers and it is one of the reasons he feels that in this matter he has been discriminated against. I think it is important for hon. members to appreciate this.
I want to point out that any member-and I hope in this particular case it will be the Speaker-who goes through this membership list will realize what a relative minority of this membership really needs the full range of the facilities that the public supply-that is, that we supply-to these gentlemen. I am not suggesting that any of them should be excluded or limited in the use of these facilities. But I am very annoyed, and I think it is a definite injustice, that this chap from the St. Catharines Standard cannot have the right to use those facilities. I want to ask you, Mr. Speaker-it has been put back to you; it is in your lap-to extend to Rodgers the use of the facilities that he has requested, and that is not the right to belong to the press gallery association. I want to ask you to do this as soon as possible. I want to tell you that if you find it impossible, this matter is going to be raised when the next session starts, and next session we are going to approach it in a much more co-ordinated cohesive way, because if the facts remain the same, as far as we are concerned an injustice will have been continued.

Mr. Chairman, as a working Canadian newspaperman of over 40 years experience in the field in Canada, I wish to state that I endorse in every word and gesture the remarks just made by the hon. member

for Port Arthur. I have sat in the press gallery of the Canadian House of Commons on three separate occasions, for three different newspapers. In every case the publisher sent a communication to the Speaker of the House of Commons asking for permission for me, as a representative of the paper, to be seated in the gallery. The publisher did not ask the members of the press gallery whether his representative could have the right to sit in the gallery. The privilege of seating people in the press gallery belongs exclusively to the Speaker and should be exercised by the Speaker. I want to go on record as endorsing the remarks of the hon. member for Port Arthur in this regard.

Mr. Chairman, I have a very few remarks to make on an entirely different subject matter. I will be very brief in connection with it. One could not have been around the parliament buildings for the last month without being impressed by the extent to which committee work has become such a very important section of the parliamentary process. For that reason I wish to say that I am very pleased indeed to see the report brought in by Mr. Speaker, which recommends the appointment of committees for the term of a parliament. I think this will have a very considerable beneficial effect on committee work.
There is one more suggestion I would like to make and it is ancillary to this recommendation. I hope that when the committee resumes, it will consider this matter. I refer to the extent to which a committee can in turn delegate its authority to subcommittees. It has been my experience that there are many matters included within the four corners of what is referred to a committee which lend themselves very well indeed to being treated by a small subcommittee of three, four, five, six or seven committee members, who in an informal way around a table, with the assistance of members of the permanent civil service, are able to direct their attention to these particular subject matters and then come back to the main committee with a report.
In my submission this is something which in due course might be worked out by a simple amendment to our standing orders which would provide-or should provide, I would hope-that a committee would have inherently the right to appoint such subcommittees. I would refer only to citation 294 of Beauchesne. I will not go into detail in this regard, Mr. Chairman, but there is raised by the contents of this paragraph, and by some research which I have carried out, some doubt as to the extent to which a committee can in fact delegate its authority to a subcommittee.

I would hope that for next year the house leader will give some consideration to establishing committees in the general terms of reference which apply, and I hope these terms of reference will include the right to appoint subcommittees for the purposes I have mentioned.

Mr. Chairman, I want to say a few words about this matter of Raymond Rodgers and the press gallery association's denial of access to certain things that he feels he requires. I am not going to go back over the evidence. It is all contained in the proceedings of the committee on privileges and elections and even in the report that committee tabled in the house yesterday. They accept the fact and restate that the facilities provided at public expense in the press gallery, and all this involves, must be under the jurisdiction of the Speaker. There is no point in going back over that.
But when we get down right to the nub of the point in question as to whether or not Rodgers should be in the press gallery, I would point out that we asked the spokesman for the press gallery during the committee meetings, "What is the criterion that is used to either accept or reject an applicant for membership in the press gallery?" Of course the witnesses referred to article 2, subsection
(a)	to which the hon. member for Port Arthur referred. I am not going to repeat it, but it provides that this right shall be restricted to persons who earn the major portion of their income through the writing or broadcasting of parliamentary or government news. When I was examining Mr. Blakely, who appeared before the committee, I put the question directly as to whether he knew anything about the income of the members of the press gallery. He said, in effect, that of course they did not look into anybody's income, and he said, "We do not care how much money they make". Yet this is the criterion they use to admit or reject people who apply for membership of and access to the press gallery and its facilities.
Under further examination the witnesses who appeared on behalf of the press gallery said that the income was not important; it was whether or not they were full-time. So I asked, "Full-time what? Full-time salary?" They said no, they did not care whether they earned $10, $40 or $200 a week; this was not important. But they had to have a letter from the managing editor or the publisher of the newspaper stating that this individual was in fact working for him full-time, or for the major part of his time. Well, Mr. Chairman, we know, as the hon. member for Port Arthur has pointed out, that there are a number of cases of members of the press gallery who

do not spend most of their time, or perhaps do not even earn most of their income reporting in the press gallery. For example we have members of the press gallery who report for agricultural papers, weeklies and even monthly agricultural publications. These people are interested in anything that takes place here that has to do with agriculture, and I presume they write about that whenever it is discussed. On the other hand, they are full-time observers and they do not know whether something respecting agriculture is going to be raised on Monday, Tuesday or Wednesday. So certainly with regard to the matter of time it cannot be said that they apply this section of their constitution to applicants. They admit that they do not apply the income part of it to applicants. Therefore I am convinced that it means nothing. They say it does not mean anything in regard to income, because they do not look into income. Nevertheless it refers to major income and says they do not care how much time is spent writing up there about the proceedings in parliament.
What actually happens is that the question of the acceptance or rejection of an applicant to the press gallery association is reduced to one of complete discretion on the part of the executive of the press gallery association. If the members of the House of Commons do not want to accept that kind of tyranny, I do not think we should allow it to go any further. I also want to say that as far as the committees work is concerned, and the recommendations they made, I think they did the Speaker an injustice, because the motion which was referred to the committee on privileges and elections was in these terms:
That the question of Raymond Rodgers' rights to use the facilities of the press gallery be referred for quick study and report back to the house on its merits by the standing committee on privileges and elections.
What the report in part said was that the committee refer the matter back to the Speaker for decision and for further study by some other committee. And this, after we had five meetings. It is a prime example of not making a decision when asked to.
To get back to Mr. Rodgers, he told us that he needs the press releases, and needs access to them quickly so that he can meet the daily deadline of the paper to which he reports. The press gallery association said that if Mr. Rodgers would come to them with a letter from his managing editor or publisher stating that he is a full-time employee of that paper, they would accept him. Mr. Rodgers, as was pointed out, is a candid man, perhaps stubborn too. Perhaps he is too stubborn to lie, which in my opinion is an attribute rather

than something to be discriminated against. He has said that he needs these facilities, which are provided at public expense.
There is a rather interesting precedent for this matter which is founded on a question of privilege set out in "Parliamentary Procedure" by Saint-Maurice, at page 669. This precedent bears a striking similarity to the present case. As a matter of fact I drew this matter to the attention of hon. members when I moved the motion which referred this matter to the committee. In this particular case an editor and proprietor of a newspaper had been commited by the Quebec legislative assembly to the custody of the sergeant-at-arms for allegedly traducing a member of his newspaper, and he remained in custody for some time. In the present case the individual has not been deprived of his physical liberties but he has been deprived of certain liberties which he had and which he ought to have to enjoy, because he relies on them to make his living. The speaker in the case cited ruled that to entitle a motion to waiver of notice and to precedence, the matter of privilege to which it relates must be urgent in point of time. This is exactly the point, Mr. Chairman: with each day of each week of each month that there is delay there is in fact a denial of liberty. The Speaker of the Quebec legislature went on to say this:
His liberation depends upon the judgment to be pronounced upon his case by the house, and as the British constitution is jealous and vigilant for the individual liberty of all who live under its sway, the question proposed is urgent in point of time...
Mr. Rodgers has been deprived of the things he thinks are his right, as a Canadian citizen and newspaperman, for several months.
I am going to close now, Mr. Chairman, because we have had much discussion on this matter; but with every day of every week of delay which deprives Mr. Rodgers of his rights there goes a serious injustice, in my view. By delay we allow the press gallery executive, or whoever is responsible for keeping Mr. Rodgers out to win their case.
Now I want to turn to one other matter. I understand an hon. member wants to speak on this subject.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for York-Humber, the hon. member for Medicine Hat and the hon. member for Port Arthur and others have expressed eloquently the feelings I have on this matter, as well I am sure as the feelings everyone in the committee have, and I think some course of action should be taken immediately to deal with it, rather than delay any longer. Accordingly I move:

Mr. Chairman, I think the committee desires, as does the house, to make a determination on this point. I will gladly withdraw the central part of my motion referring to the recommendation that Raymond Spencer Rodgers have access to the facilities of the press gallery, so that it would read:
That the committee rise, report progress, and ask leave to sit again later this day.
Then when we rise and report progress with Mr. Speaker in the chair the house would be in a position to deal with the matter.
The Depuiy Chairman: Then the procedure would be for the hon. member for Skeena to withdraw his present motion and to move a motion that the committee rise.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Perhaps I might take a moment of the committee's time, while the hon. member is producing his motion, to raise a question which the hon. gentleman might answer before he goes further. It is true that making this motion and giving leave to sit again does not impede the business of the house except for the brief period-if it was a brief period-during which the motion would be before the Speaker. friends is, I regret, not here at this moment. He will be able to give us some guidance on this point. Indeed, I feel this is one of the occasions when we ought to send for him. But I will try, in my poor way, to fill in. It does seem to me that it would not be possible for the house to do anything of a substantive nature with the Speaker in the chair without a substantive motion of some description being before it. That would require unanimous consent in the circumstances which exist today. Perhaps a good deal of the time of the house and the committee could be saved if, before the hon. member went to the length of moving his motion, he would tell us what kind of motion he would propose to make after the committee has risen. Then he could ascertain from those of us who are here-and I do not think the composition of this chamber is likely to change materially in the course of the next few minutes- whether he would get unanimous consent for his motion after the Speaker has resumed the chair. Needless to say, I am in a mood to cooperate as far as it is possible to do so. But the hon. gentleman, who is very ingenious, has presented us with a surprise and perhaps he could tell us what the surprise is going to be before he makes his motion for the committee to rise.

Perhaps I could deal with that. I may say that if there is any ingenuity on my part it is only because I have attentively watched the Secretary of State over the months, both in his present capacity and before that. Undoubtedly the motion would have to be a substantive motion and it would require unanimous consent, since notice is difficult to give at this late stage in the proceedings. The motion to which I would be glad to have the house give its approval is as follows:
That the Sergeant-at-Arms, pursuant to standing order No. 88, be instructed to grant pro tern a card admitting Raymond Rodgers to the press gallery of this house.

speechtext: Did the hon. member for Edmonton West wish to say something?
As far as procedure is concerned, obviously this would be a debatable motion. It is a substantive motion and would require notice unless unanimous consent were given.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I think everybody recognizes that, unless there were unanimous consent when the Speaker was in the chair, the Speaker could not entertain the motion. I suggested that we find out now, before the motion to rise was made, whether there would be unanimous consent to the motion being made. This would not imply that we would support the motion.
On that point, I think it would be quite improper to ask what would be the desire of the house with the chairman in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I should like to point out that the procedure we are embarking on now is somewhat irregular. The Chair is not very disposed to rule in advance. The duty of the Chair is to rule on what happens, not on what might happen.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I defer to Your Honour and to experts like the hon. member for Edmonton West in these matters. It only seemed to me that if there was a plainly negative feeling expressed in the committee it might save a little time. However, perhaps it would be better if the hon. member were to put his motion, which he has a perfect right to do at any time, that the committee rise and report progress. We can see what happens when his motion is made. That does not imply that the other motion would be acceptable or that unanimous consent would be given if the committee should decide to rise. I may say that I would prefer-and I offer this suggestion to the hon. member-to let this stand over until we have disposed of the estimates and we have risen in the normal course of things. There will be a certain interval of time, then, during which the government has undertaken to allow one or two other matters to be brought up and I would certainly be willing to see that before we went to the other place the hon. member, or the hon. member for Medicine Hat, were given an opportunity to ascertain whether there was unanimous consent to consider the matter at that time. This would avoid any interruption of our present proceedings. If that would be satisfactory I would certainly give such an undertaking. This could be done after the appropriation bill had been disposed of and before we came to the other matters. The hon. gentleman could seek unanimous consent at that time and we would be able to continue.

There is one further problem which I should like to refer to the Secretary of State. If the committee should rise, and if the Speaker were to come back into the chair, is the minister sure as to how the house would get back into committee of supply?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I understand that the hon. gentleman was going to move that we rise, report progress and ask leave to sit later this day. So that problem is taken care of. But the position would be safeguarded by the suggestion I have made, and I hope the two hon. members who are particularly concerned with this matter will be disposed to accept it.

My approach to matters of this nature is not how we are bound by the rules, but whether we can take a reasonable course toward reaching a solution. That is what I have in mind, rather than what happened in 1890 or on various occasions in the past. I think the hon. member for Medicine Hat and others would agree to the course suggested by the Secretary of State, that is that we should wait until we have concluded the business before the committee, then rise in the normal course and ascertain what the views of the house are at that time. I would therefore ask leave to withdraw the motion which I placed before you a while ago, Mr. Chairman.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am most grateful to both hon. members for being accommodating with regard to a matter about which they obviously feel strongly.

Since, later on, he may be in the chair and it may be difficult for him to express any views, may I ask the Speaker whether he has any comments to make on the questions I raised with regard to the Rodgers case?

Yes, I have quite a few comments to make. Up to the present time there have been nine speakers, all raising matters of considerable interest. Certainly, they are matters of great interest to me. I do not "think it would be fair at this time to concentrate on one subject. I would prefer to make a general statement at the end.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words about the index of Hansard.
I wish to suggest that those people who receive Hansard on the basis of lists sent in by members should receive the index as well. I know that people who subscribe to Hansard can get the index by paying an extra dollar, but many members send Hansard to schools and local libraries and I should like to suggest that the index go along with the regular subscription where the names are submitted by members.
My other point has to do with the indexing staff. My office is located next to the indexing branch, both English and French, and I notice that they seem to put in very long hours and very frequently work on the week end and particularly at night. It seems to me there is a very large amount of indexing to be done these days because of the increase in questions on the order paper and the many speeches being made. I have the impression that branch is understaffed and I should like to have this situation investigated.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to bring up again at this time a matter I raised earlier with regard to the capitalization and punctuation methods of the Hansard editors. I should like to bring it up now because I have noted that the Senate Hansard editors apparently follow, to my mind, a more literate and a more proper system of capitalization. This was brought quite sharply to my attention when I found that the hon. gentlemen in the other place had been discussing the same thing I had been discussing in the speech about which I complained. I refer to the capitalization of "international monetary fund" which the Senate Hansard editors quite rightly capitalized, as it is a definite organization and which our editor refused flatly to capitalize, leaving it in a perfectly ridiculous situation in that the reference might be merely to an abstract concept of a world fund of some sort. I should like to suggest at this time that Mr. Speaker take under advisement a review of the methods of capitalization and punctuation in the editing of Hansard because today they are far from satisfactory to anyone who has any care for the use of the English language.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall item No. 1 carry?

Before it carries, Mr. Chairman, I thought Mr. Speaker had some comments to make on some of the suggestions that have been made. I think some of them are fairly current and warrant immediate attention.

Mr. Chairman, this is one of the few but very pleasant opportunities I have to say something in the house in the present circumstances. I should like to seize the opportunity and begin by conveying my appreciation of the good work that the staff of the Speaker has done in rather trying circumstances, shall we say, since September 30. In that connection I want to single out particularly the Clerk, who has carried a very severe load since September 30, Mr. Montgomery who, due to a little overwork, shall we say, had to leave us for a few weeks, and Mr. Dubroy who has been of tremendous assistance. The three gentlemen at the table in the centre of the Commons, as you may well judge, have carried more than their fair share of work this session.
I should also like to mention the Sergeant-at-Arms who is burdened with a great deal of detail, some of which has been referred to today. Then there are the various heads of departments, the head of Hansard, the interpreters, with whom we work very closely, although they do not actually come under our jurisdiction, the head and clerks of the committees branch-and I think all members

Supply-Legislation
know the difficulties under which they have been working this session-the constables, the pages and all other members of our staff.
I should also like to thank members of the house for their constant co-operation, which has been very necessary and very much appreciated by me. At this time, although it may be a little forward, I should like to thank members once again for the honour they have done me in sustaining me as Speaker on more than one occasion.
I would be remiss if I did not refer to the Deputy Speaker and the deputy chairman of committees who is in the chair now. They too have carried quite a burden.
It will be seen from what I have said, I think, and from the discussion this afternoon that times are changing in the House of Commons, and I am all for change. Eleven members this afternoon have shown a great deal of interest in the organization of the House of Commons, and I will not say that I am unsympathetic in any way with many of the views presented, but on the contrary the more constructive criticism we get the better I like it. With that in mind we have already been making a few changes. Things do not move quite as fast in the public service as they do in private organizations and I confess to periods of frustration, just the same as some hon. members. But we are building up a good working team in the Speaker's establishment and I am rather proud of it at the moment. We hope to improve.
Many questions have been raised. I am sure hon. members do not expect me to deal with them all in detail; but to show that I do have some comprehension of some of the problems I would refer to the fact that, for example, reference was made by the hon. member for Timiskaming to staff, and in particular to the protective staff and the fact that we have 72 members on that staff. One of the new problems which have arisen within the last three to five years is what to do with the increasing volume of tourist traffic on the hill. Five years ago we had 500 tourists a day. In July and August this year we ran between 6,000 and 7,000 a day. All of them want to get into the galleries. This is a new problem and it points up that times are changing and a new approach has to be considered.
Other questions had to do with the translation bureau. This morning I had the opportunity of visiting what I admit are very poor quarters that they are occupying at the present time. Already I have dictated a letter at 12.05 p.m. today to the Sergeant-at-Arms to raise this question immediately and see what we can do about it.

There is the question of committees and whether or not the messengers should be trained to operate the radio facilities. This matter has already been discussed on two or three occasions, and again another letter was dictated today with a view to seeing how we can improve the facilities for the next session.
There were a great many other questions. The hon. member for Timiskaming referred to the fact that the internal economy commission was perhaps outdated and should be replaced by a joint party committee to help the Speaker. This is a very interesting suggestion. It was dealt with more or less fully in 1962 by the hon. member for Skeena. I have the record here and I have read it very carefully.
However, I would point out to the hon. member that it is not up to the Speaker to decide this matter. The Speaker is bound by the House of Commons Act, which makes it a statutory matter. If the hon. member wishes to change the act, let him do so, but certainly the Speaker has no power in that regard. Section 16 of the House of Commons Act reads as follows;
The governor in council shall appoint four members of the Queen's privy council for Canada who are also members of the House of Commons, who, with the Speaker of the House of Commons, shall be commissioners for the purposes of this section and sections 17 and 18.
It might interest hon. members to know that the members of the internal economy commission are the Minister of Justice, the Minister of Finance, the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the Secretary of State.
With regard to television and radio facilities, I will have more to say about that in connection with the press gallery. Someone mentioned research facilities. This is one of the things I am extremely keen about and perhaps I am giving my personal views but surely once a year I am entitled to do that. We have in mind to review from the ground up or from the top down-it does not matter .-the library of parliament. We feel that at the present time the library of parliament, good as it is, is not necessarily fulfilling the function for which it was set up. We have in mind the congressional library in Washington and the facilities provided in the United Kingdom. For that reason I have already on the desk a report on certain improvements which could be made. This question, of course, will be considered by the committee on procedure and organization which has been set up.
In so far as the Hansard staff is concerned, their salaries and numbers, I may say that this year we have been in particular difficulty as a result of the number of committees, the

level of salaries which are paid, and difficulties in recruiting the staff. For that reason, the question of whether tape recording should replace the present system was referred to a committee.
Several other questions have been brought up today. There was the question of telecommunications raised by the hon. member for Lapointe. I understand that at the moment the internal economy commissioners have not reached any conclusion as to whether it would be a good or a bad thing to pay for the telegrams, long distance calls and all the rest of it. I am sure that hon. members will appreciate that they have not been too badly treated as of the moment.
In so far as the recognition problem is concerned, the hon. gentleman who raised it is not here so I am going to take advantage of the fact and not deal with the question.
Various other points were raised, not the least of which was the one raised by the hon. member for Port Arthur, joined by the hon. members for York-Humber, Medicine Hat, Skeena and one or two others. This question related to Raymond Rodgers and the press gallery. In view of the discussion here this afternoon, which I found very helpful and useful, I must say that I think hon. members know that I am not at all unsympathetic to the person concerned. I doubt if he has received as much attention from many other people as he has received from me during the last few months. The question is not an easy one to decide, and should not be decided on the basis of emotion or personality but on the basis of principle. For that reason I have told him, and told anyone who wanted to listen, that in due course when the principle has been established in the proper way and all factors have been considered, that will be the right time to render a judgment.
In so far as the press gallery is concerned, Mr. Rodgers is not alone in complaining. Many members of the press gallery are complaining constantly about the space problem. I am well aware of the conditions under which they work. I am well aware also of the fact that within the last few years the numbers in the press gallery have increased from 30 to about 110 or 120. This, in part, results from the development of communications by radio and television. The point is that the system under which we have been working up to the present time, vis-a-vis the press gallery, is very much out of date. Only yesterday I had the president, and perhaps the past president, of the press gallery in to discuss the constitution. I said that the constitution needs to be re-examined, reassessed and brought up to date. The same remarks apply to the bylaws under the constitution.

The question of space is a very pressing one. We thought at one time the taking over of the west block would be the answer to the problem. However, the problem seems to get worse every day. One idea that we have toyed with is that of dividing the membership of the gallery into two categories, those who are connected with daily papers and those who are connected with weekly papers or magazines. At the moment we have under reservation considerable space in the west block. We are trying to negotiate a solution between the press gallery and the Department of Public Works which will be of use to both sides.
There is also the question of visiting pressmen from other countries and other capitals. They arrive here and there is no place to entertain them. Perhaps the members of the press should construct their own building, as is done in Washington. Perhaps the owners of the large newspapers should, themselves, look into this problem and assist the rest of us.
In any event, it may be possible to work out a solution by which the members of the press gallery would get more space by splitting them into two parts, the daily and weekly or magazine sections, and thus make better facilities available. Amongst the better facilities, I include the need for a room in the basement or some other convenient place in this building to be used as a television and radio studio. I think all of us agree that it is ridiculous that the C.B.C. should go to the expense of hauling equipment up here every time they want to televise some proceedings, thus cluttering up the halls. It should be possible for members to go to a room downstairs for television or radio broadcasts. This is another thing we have in mind.
If I may summarize the whole question, I may say that the problem of the press gallery will be thoroughly considered by the new committee on parliamentary procedure and organization. I have already suggested that we set up immediately a small subcommittee, as was suggested by the hon. member for Peace River, to do the necessary research on this problem of space, constitution, bylaws, membership and all the rest of it. So far as I am concerned, until I receive a carefully thought out and well documented report which has been discussed with our advisers, I do not believe it would be right to jump in and give an emotional decision, no matter what I may think personally, nor is it the right time to give a decision on this Rodgers case. It may be decided later on. You cannot act as judge and jury at the same time.
I believe I have covered most of the points that were raised this afternoon in a very cursory way. There are a great many problems. One thing I should like to bring to the

Supply-Legislation
attention of hon. members is the desire which I know you have, and which certainly the Speaker has, of making a complete review of the Speaker's establishment. This is long overdue, for some of the reasons I have given this afternoon. Things get out of date when built-in systems of doing things continue from year to year. The purpose of setting up the committee on procedure and parliamentary organization was precisely to examine the standing orders of the house, try to modernize and streamline them for what it may be worth, and the most important factor involved is the modernizing of the way in which the institutions work in the house. I feel that inasmuch as we are in an industrial age, in a mechanical age, we need every mechanical gadget we can get to speed things up; that is the way things are done. I told you that I thought the library should be carefully examined. I told you I thought the committee system needed to be carefully reexamined. I have always said, from the beginning, that the committees are too large and smaller committees, as suggested by the hon. member for Peace River, are more effective. Well, this idea may be right or it may be wrong.
These are some of the outstanding problems, and anything which will make parliament more effective, which will create a better image vis-a-vis the public, must be considered and must be brought into force. This is the purpose of setting up the parliamentary committee on procedure and reform, if I could call it that. I assure you that the committee, consisting as it does of highly qualified members experienced in this house, with sufficient finances to find the necessary papers to study, with a desire to examine the system at work south of the border and the source of parliamentary inspiration in the United Kingdom, with all of these things and with these ideas floating around, will surprise me if it does not bring about a revolution in many of the procedures which we are following at the present time, something which is long overdue.

I am sure the applause indicates the feeling of everyone in relation to the reception of the comments by Mr. Speaker. It is always a bit inhibiting, because we have the highest regard for that office and for the person who holds it, to get involved in a controversial debate over matters under the jurisdiction of Mr. Speaker.
There is one point I would like to follow up, and it deals with the question of research assistance. The only research assistance that is available at the moment is that referred to in standing order 87 which says:
It is the duty of the joint law clerks of the house to assist members...in drafting legislation-

I think it is particularly important to draw attention to the words "joint law clerks''. The background for this, as was mentioned earlier by the hon. member for Timiskaming is such that there should be joint law clerks, one familiar with the civil code as it is in Quebec, and the other familiar with the common law as it is in other parts of Canada. It also is connected with the two founding races who entered confederation, and is connected with the current interest in bilingualism and biculturalism.
Unfortunately we do not have joint law clerks. We have one law clerk in the person of Dr. Maurice Ollivier who is, I am sure, well known to everybody in the house and who has appeared before a number of committees. Dr. Ollivier for the last few years- I could not say offhand how many, but eight or ten years-has filled the position set out in standing order 87 as "joint law clerks". I submit he is not. He is a singular person, and his background is that of the civil code of Quebec. I submit there should be another person appointed to participate with Dr. Ollivier in filling the position stipulated by standing order 87 of joint law clerks, so that there will be an English speaking and a French speaking person filling his office, having equal stature, status and standing, and so that members can go to whomever they choose to assist in the preparation of bills.
This matter was of great concern to many hon. members before the summer recess took place. It was discussed at a variety of meetings in which a number of people participated. We hoped that before the summer recess ended a solution would be found and that there would be appointed joint law clerks.
Speaking personally, I have a bit of a grievance with respect to this because the experience I have had with respect to Dr. Ollivier in assisting in the preparation of bills, has not been too good. I have only had occasion twice to go to him specifically to seek assistance in the preparation of bills. In one case he refused, saying it was not possible. In another case he prepared a bill for me which I filed and presented to the house. I subsequently discovered there were three errors in that particular bill and I am glad it did not come up for second reading, because it would have been a bit embarrassing for me to deal with a bill containing three errors, incidentally all of them on the same page.
I draw this to the attention of the committee because I think hon. members are not getting full assistance from the law clerk of the law branch, for the simple reason there is not in that office two people, one of French speaking descent, familiar with the civil code

of Quebec, and another of English descent familiar with the common law of England and Canada, both having equal stature and status. This situation has been going on too long so far as I am concerned, and I hope Mr. Speaker will make a decision about it within the next few moments and indicate that there are going to be joint law clerks as provided by the standing order, so that every one will be on an equal footing.

This is a far more serious matter than meets the eye and I hope Mr. Speaker will reply.
I would like to make just a few remarks as I realize time is passing. First of all, I want to say I have the highest confidence in and most pleasant relations with Dr. Ollivier.
Hear, hear.

He is, as is well known, besides being a good attorney a professor of constitutional law at Ottawa University, and I can testify that in my short term as Speaker so far, he has been of tremendous use to me personally, both with regard to preparing bills and opinions, and advice generally. As an attorney, myself, of a fair amount of experience, both in business and in law, I value his views.
I realize there are difficulties in that department. The hon. member and myself have discussed this on more than one occasion. I have done my best to try and regulate some of these difficulties, not too successfully; but while there is life there is hope. It is one of the problems that I referred to inferentially when I said there were a lot of problems in the Speaker's establishment; but this is one problem I am going to refer to the special committee. It is their job to examine it and help and advise me in reaching a conclusion. As of the moment I just want to say, so far as the gentleman referred to is concerned that he has my full confidence and will continue to have it so long as I am Speaker.
Could I ask the intentions of Mr. Speaker to maintain the office of joint law clerks?

That is asking for a decision. I am not afraid to make decisions, but I am afraid of not making the right decision, and that takes time and consideration. As I have said, it is a difficult problem to answer and it is one which is under close study at present. As to whether there should or should not be more than one, I am going to seek the advice of this special committee which
Supply-Legislation
was set up to examine these problems. If we are going to use the parliamentary system at all and if we are not to have dictatorship- even though as I say I am not afraid of making decisions, I have made them all my life-we should use this committee. It was set up to consider these problems, and surely courtesy and justice dictate that the committee be consulted so that it may advise the Speaker. That is the democratic way to do things.

I was very happy to hear Mr. Speaker say that this committee, of which he is chairman, will introduce great reforms in the house. It is about time. However, I am sure hon. members will recognize one problem has not been touched upon, and that concerns the page boys, our great helpers. Of necessity they are enrolled in their own schools up to noon hour. That is half a day; and when they work here for the rest of the day they are denied the education that they should have, with the result that in a great many cases they drop out of school at a very early age.
Surely the time has now come when we should consider a completely new system of page boys, through which their education could be provided here, possibly along with living accommodation, and then page boys could come here from all over Canada and not of necessity just from Ottawa and Hull. I would like to bring this to the attention of the Speaker and his committee. It is a problem that deserves consideration as quickly as possible.

Mr. Chairman, just a few brief remarks to thank the Speaker and the Clerk for the co-operation they have extended to me and the readiness with which they received my suggestion to put French and English titles on the books and reference records on the table of the house.
I would not miss this opportunity either to mention that the two preceding Speakers have always been very kind to me and have always shown their willingness to implement my suggestions to the effect that both in the house and on parliament hill bilingualism be more and more widely recognized.
Item agreed to.
